- https://rust-analyzer.github.io/blog/2020/07/20/three-architectures-for-responsive-ide.html — confirmed
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astral-sh/ruff/main/crates/ty_project/src/db.rs (`ProjectDatabase`) — confirmed
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/astral-sh/ruff/main/crates/ty/src/lib.rs (CLI main loop, `salsa::Cancelled::catch`, `freeze`) — confirmed
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/biomejs/biome/main/crates/biome_service/src/workspace.rs (`Workspace` trait) — confirmed
- https://salsa-rs.github.io/salsa/overview.html — confirmed
- https://salsa-rs.github.io/salsa/reference/durability.html — confirmed
- https://docs.rs/salsa/latest/salsa/ (item list: `Database`, `Storage`, `StorageHandle`, `Cancelled`, `Durability`, `CancellationToken`, `Revision`, `Setter`) — confirmed
- https://tree-sitter.github.io/tree-sitter/using-parsers/3-advanced-parsing.html (`ts_tree_edit`, `ts_tree_copy`, thread-safety) — confirmed
- https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/struct.BufWriter.html (flush-on-drop swallows errors) — confirmed
- https://docs.rs/grep-searcher/latest/grep_searcher/ (`Sink` vs `grep-printer`) — confirmed
- rowan `SyntaxNode: !Sync`, thread-local free list, `GreenNode` is the sendable half — likely (rust-analyzer `docs/dev/syntax.md` via mirror + rowan issue #15; not re-read from canonical upstream path)
- Hammer, Khoo, Hicks, Foster, "Adapton: Composable, Demand-Driven Incremental Computation," PLDI 2014 pp. 156–166 — likely (abstract + artifact page; full PDF not fetched)
- oxc `Allocator` / allocator-pool reuse rationale (oxc-project/oxc issue #20513, `oxc_allocator` docs) — likely (summarized, not read verbatim)
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/golang/tools/master/gopls/doc/design/design.md — confirmed (contains the long-lived-process rationale; does **not** contain the Session/View/Snapshot hierarchy that `06-daemon-architecture.md` §3 attributes to gopls)
- LSP 3.17/3.18 `completionItem/resolve`, `workspaceSymbol/resolve`, `resolve_support`, `$/progress` partial results — likely (spec text via search summary, not fetched verbatim)
- Ambient-context / shared-global-object critiques (beberlei.de "Explicit Global State with Context Objects", ilovedotnet ambient-context anti-pattern) — likely (secondary, non-Rust)

## Findings

1. **rust-analyzer's split is exactly two types, and the asymmetry is `&mut` vs `&`.** Verbatim from `crates/ide/src/lib.rs`: `pub struct AnalysisHost { db: RootDatabase }` with `pub fn analysis(&self) -> Analysis { Analysis { db: self.db.clone() } }` and `pub fn apply_change(&mut self, change: ChangeWithProcMacros) -> Duration`. `pub struct Analysis { db: RootDatabase }` — same field, different capability. The architecture doc states the rule in one line: "`AnalysisHost` is a state to which you can transactionally `apply_change`. `Analysis` is an immutable snapshot of the state." Snapshot creation is an `Arc`-level clone, O(1). Source: rust-analyzer `crates/ide/src/lib.rs`, `docs/book/src/contributing/architecture.md:216-217`.

2. **`AnalysisHost` also exposes raw access, publicly, next to the curated façade.** `pub fn raw_database(&self) -> &RootDatabase` and `pub fn raw_database_mut(&mut self) -> &mut RootDatabase` are public methods on `AnalysisHost`. But the same doc says of the `ide` API: "syntax trees and hir types are generally absent from the API (but are used heavily in the implementation)." So the precedent is: raw access exists as a named escape hatch on the *host*, while the *snapshot's* query surface stays POD. Source: `crates/ide/src/lib.rs`, `architecture.md:212`.

3. **Cancellation in rust-analyzer is a consequence of Salsa's shared mutable memo table, not of being a server.** "The salsa database maintains a global revision counter. When applying a change, salsa bumps this counter and waits until all other threads using salsa finish. If a thread does salsa-based computation and notices that the counter is incremented, it panics with a special value (see `Canceled::throw`). That is, rust-analyzer requires unwinding. `ide` is the boundary where the panic is caught and transformed into a `Result<T, Cancelled>`." Note the mechanism: a write *waits for readers to die*. That is a property of a mutable store shared by snapshots — not a property of long-lived sessions in general. Source: `architecture.md:377-388`.

4. **ty confirms the waiting-for-readers mechanic in salsa 3.** `ProjectDatabase` carries `storage: salsa::Storage<ProjectDatabase>` with the comment "This field must be the last because we use `trigger_cancellation` to drop all other storage references," and `system_mut` does `Arc::get_mut(&mut self.system).expect("ref count should be 1 because `trigger_cancellation` drops all other DB references.")`. So in a Salsa design, taking `&mut` on the database is a runtime operation that **invalidates every outstanding snapshot** and panics on unwinding readers. Source: `astral-sh/ruff` `crates/ty_project/src/db.rs`.

5. **ty is a one-shot CLI and still uses a session object — plus a `freeze()` fast path for exactly the non-daemon case.** From `crates/ty/src/lib.rs`: `let mut db = ProjectDatabase::fallible(project_metadata, system)?;` then `if !watch { ruff_db::disable_lru(&mut db); } db.freeze_open_files(); if !watch && matches!(mode, MainLoopMode::Check) && ... { db.freeze(); }`. It then does `let db = db.clone(); rayon::spawn(move || { match salsa::Cancelled::catch(|| { db.check_with_reporter(&mut reporter) ...`. Three facts fall out: (a) the database is `#[derive(Clone)]` and the clone is the snapshot, sent across threads to rayon; (b) a one-shot run explicitly *turns off* incremental machinery (LRU disabled, inputs frozen to high durability) because nothing will change; (c) cancellation is retained even in the CLI, but only to service Ctrl+C. Source: `astral-sh/ruff` `crates/ty/src/lib.rs`, `crates/ty_project/src/db.rs`.

6. **Biome takes the opposite shape: `&self` everywhere, no snapshot type, RPC-shaped params/results.** `pub trait Workspace: Send + Sync + RefUnwindSafe` with `open_project(OpenProjectParams) -> Result<OpenProjectResult, WorkspaceError>`, `open_file(OpenFileParams)`, `change_file(ChangeFileParams)`, `close_file`, `pull_diagnostics(PullDiagnosticsParams)`, `format_file`, `go_to_definition`. All methods take `&self` despite mutating internal state — the source comments that "the workspace is allowed to internally cache data across calls," with open documents as GC roots. The reason for the `&self`/params-struct shape is stated in the source: "the `Workspace` trait is eventually intended to also be implemented for a potential `WorkspaceClient` type and to operate on a remote workspace server through a transport layer." Biome pays for this with a `RetryingWorkspace<W>` wrapper and `retry_on_pending_write()` — i.e. it reintroduces cancellation handling at the call site because it discarded the borrow-checker's help. Source: `biomejs/biome` `crates/biome_service/src/workspace.rs`.

7. **A change enters rust-analyzer as a value carrying content, not a list of dirty paths.** `pub struct FileChange { pub roots: Option<Vec<SourceRoot>>, pub files_changed: Vec<(FileId, Option<String>)>, pub crate_graph: Option<CrateGraphBuilder> }`, applied by `apply()`. `Option<String>` is the new text; `None` means deleted. It is a batch — many files, roots, and the crate graph in one transaction — which is what makes "transactionally apply_change" true. Source: `crates/base-db/src/change.rs`.

8. **Durability is three tiers and is assigned per-input at change-application time, by provenance, not by rate of change measured at runtime.** `FileChange::apply` sets library source roots to `Durability::MEDIUM`, local roots to `Durability::LOW`, library file text to `Durability::HIGH`, local file text to `Durability::LOW`. The mechanism (from the rust-analyzer blog): "we go from a single version number to a version vector. E.g., if we have three durability levels `(volatile, normal, durable)`, then our version is a tuple of three numbers," and "incrementing `normal` increments *both* `volatile` and `normal`." The measured payoff: validating after a local edit without durability cost "about 300ms" traversing stdlib queries; with durability, "we notice that the durable version is the same … and skip over the entire query subgraph." Source: `crates/base-db/src/change.rs`, https://rust-analyzer.github.io/blog/2023/07/24/durable-incrementality.html.

9. **rust-analyzer's own framing is that laziness, not incrementality, is what buys the speed.** "It's not the incrementality that makes an IDE fast. Rather, it's laziness — the ability to skip huge swaths of code altogether." This is the single most load-bearing sentence for Monokl, which currently eagerly `par_iter()`s the whole tree in `WorkspaceIndex::build` before answering any query. Source: https://rust-analyzer.github.io/blog/2020/07/20/three-architectures-for-responsive-ide.html.

10. **Adapton, in one paragraph.** Adapton (Hammer, Khoo, Hicks, Foster, PLDI 2014) formalizes *demand-driven* incremental computation: the program is a graph of thunks, and change propagation is driven lazily from *observers* pulling on outputs rather than eagerly from inputs pushing invalidation forward. Its central structural move is "an explicit separation between inner, incremental computations and outer observers," which lets inner computations be reused more liberally because nothing is recomputed until something actually demands it. Salsa's demand-driven query model is the direct descendant of this; the practical consequence for an API is that the session object should expose *queries*, not a "rebuild everything now" verb.

11. **The `ide` serialization rule, verbatim, with the reasoning.** "In Rust, it is easy (often too easy) to add serialization to any type by adding `#[derive(Serialize)]`. This easiness is misleading — serializable types impose significant backwards compatibility constraints. If a type is serializable, then it is a part of some IPC boundary. You often don't control the other side of this boundary, so changing serializable types is hard. For this reason, the types in `ide`, `base_db` and below are not serializable by design." Paired with: "**Architecture Invariant:** `rust-analyzer` is the only crate that knows about LSP and JSON serialization. If you want to expose a data structure `X` from ide to LSP, don't make it serializable. Instead, create a serializable counterpart in `rust-analyzer` crate and manually convert between the two." The worked example given is `rust-project.json`: "it doesn't include `CrateGraph` as is. Instead, it creates a `CrateGraph` by calling appropriate constructing functions." Source: `architecture.md:232-234, 505-517`.

12. **But the `ide` API is nevertheless *shaped* as if it were serializable.** "**Architecture Invariant:** `ide` crate's API is build out of POD types with public fields. The API uses editor's terminology, it talks about offsets and string labels rather than in terms of definitions or types. It is effectively the view in MVC and viewmodel in MVVM. All arguments and return types are conceptually serializable." So the rule is not "keep the API rich and opaque" — it is "keep the API flat and dumb, and *still* don't derive serde on it." Source: `architecture.md:208-212`.

13. **Monokl today violates finding 11 wholesale.** `docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md` §4 opens with `use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};` and every public type — `SymbolKind`, `Visibility`, `SymbolEntry`, `DependencyRecord`, `DependencyBinding`, `BindingKind`, `WorkspaceOptions`, `ExtractRequest` — carries `#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]` with `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` and `skip_serializing_if` attributes. These same types are simultaneously (a) the public library API, (b) the `.monokl/cache.json` on-disk format, and (c) the agent-facing JSON wire shape. Three independent compatibility clocks on one struct. `skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none"` on `SymbolEntry::owner` is a *presentation* decision that is currently welded onto the *analysis* type. Source: monokl spec §4, §16 (`analysis/persist.rs`).

14. **Monokl's snapshot problem is already half-solved and doesn't need Salsa.** `FileAnalysis` is owned, `Arc`-shared, and content-hash keyed (`ARCHITECTURE.md`: "everything in it is owned data … This is a hard rule, not a style preference: it's what lets `FileAnalysis` be cached, shared across threads via `Arc`, and outlive the parse call that produced it"). `WorkspaceIndex` is a plain struct of `Vec`/`FxHashMap`/`ImportGraph`/`SymbolIndex` built once by `WorkspaceIndex::build` and never mutated afterward. An `Arc<WorkspaceIndex>` is therefore already a valid immutable snapshot with no memo table behind it. Source: monokl `ARCHITECTURE.md`, spec §19.

15. **Long-lived embedding is not something the parsers underneath Monokl offer.** tree-sitter is the only one with a real incremental-reparse API: `ts_tree_edit()` with `TSInputEdit { start_byte, start_point, old_end_byte/point, new_end_byte/point }`, then re-calling `ts_parser_parse()` with the old tree, which "internally shares structure with the old tree." It also documents a threading constraint: `TSTree` "instances are not thread-safe" — you must `ts_tree_copy()` (an atomic refcount bump) before concurrent use. `ra_ap_syntax`/rowan splits into a thread-safe `GreenNode` and a `!Sync` `SyntaxNode` that uses `Rc` and thread-local free lists, so red trees cannot live in a shared snapshot at all — you send `(GreenNode, Range)` and rebuild. oxc has no persistent-parse-state API; its long-lived story is *allocator reuse* ("re-using an existing `Allocator` avoids these costs" of malloc/free per parse), which is amortization, not incrementality. Sources: tree-sitter advanced-parsing docs; rowan/`ra_ap_syntax` (likely); oxc-project/oxc #20513 (likely).

16. **The "raw facts vs. formatted output" split has strong precedent inside Monokl's own dependency tree.** `grep-searcher`'s crate docs: the `Searcher` is "principally responsible for managing the consumption of bytes from a source and applying a `Matcher` over those bytes in an efficient way," while a `Sink` "describes how callers receive search results" and may be "trivially simple" or "extraordinarily complex, such as the `Standard` printer found in the `grep-printer` crate." ripgrep — the tool Monokl already borrows its text prefilter from — ships the raw search engine and the budgeted/coloured/context-managed printer as two separate crates. LSP does the same thing on the wire: `completionItem/resolve` and `workspaceSymbol/resolve` exist because "computing full completion items is expensive," so the cheap batch comes back first and depth is pulled per-item, gated by the `completion_item.resolve_support` capability listing which properties may be deferred. Sources: docs.rs `grep_searcher`; LSP 3.17/3.18 (likely).

17. **The library-level critique of session objects is about *ambient* sessions, not *explicit* ones.** The recurring complaint in the literature is the ambient-context / shared-global-object pattern: state reached through a static accessor with "no clear owner," therefore "a non-deterministic and permanent lifecycle," untestable and racy. The stated remedies are that a context object should be immutable, not a singleton, and explicitly passed. `Workspace::open(opts) -> Workspace` handed to the caller as an owned value satisfies all three; the anti-pattern would be a `monokl::global_workspace()` or a lazily-initialized static cache behind the free functions. Note that Monokl's current free-function API is *closer* to the anti-pattern than the proposed session object is, because the process-local `DashMap` cache and `.monokl/cache.json` are already ambient state that `search()`/`symbols()`/`dependents()` reach implicitly. Sources: secondary (beberlei.de, ilovedotnet) — likely.

18. **An explicit flush is the documented Rust idiom, and `Drop` is documented as insufficient.** `std::io::BufWriter`: "It is critical to call `flush` before `BufWriter<W>` is dropped. Though dropping will attempt to flush the contents of the buffer, any errors that happen in the process of dropping will be ignored. Calling `flush` ensures that the buffer is empty and thus dropping will not even attempt file operations." Monokl currently calls `crate::analysis::persist::flush(root, config_hash)?` as the last statement of `WorkspaceIndex::build` — i.e. inside index construction, where a query-only caller cannot decline it and a caller that builds two indices flushes twice. Sources: std docs; monokl spec §19 line `crate::analysis::persist::flush(root, config_hash)?;`.

19. **rust-analyzer's snapshot is not just the analysis — it is a struct of `Arc`s cloned in one place.** `GlobalState::snapshot()` builds `GlobalStateSnapshot { config: Arc::clone(&self.config), workspaces: Arc::clone(&self.workspaces), analysis: self.analysis_host.analysis(), vfs: Arc::clone(&self.vfs), … }`, and there is an explicit `impl std::panic::UnwindSafe for GlobalStateSnapshot {}` — required because the cancellation design (finding 3) unwinds through it. If a design has no cancellation, it needs no `UnwindSafe` assertion. Source: `crates/rust-analyzer/src/global_state.rs:214-230, 574-588`.

20. **One citation in Monokl's own spec does not check out against the primary source.** `docs/spec/06-daemon-architecture.md` §3 states: "rust-analyzer's `GlobalState`/Salsa snapshot model and gopls's Session→View→Snapshot hierarchy both solve this the same way." The rust-analyzer half is confirmed (finding 19). The gopls half is not present in `gopls/doc/design/design.md`, which argues only for a long-running process with in-memory caching and explicitly no persistent disk cache ("Persistent disk caches are very expensive to maintain"). The Session/View/Snapshot hierarchy is real in gopls' implementation (`internal/lsp/cache`), but the cited design doc does not contain it. Source: `golang/tools` `gopls/doc/design/design.md`.

## Verdict on proposed changes

**Proposal 1 — `Workspace` session object as primary API: confirm, with a required refinement to two types, not one.**

Every comparable system converges on a session object even when it is not a daemon: rust-analyzer (`AnalysisHost`), ty's one-shot CLI (`ProjectDatabase`, finding 5), Biome (`Workspace`). The refinement is that a single `Workspace` on which all queries hang is the shape Biome chose, and Biome pays for it with `RetryingWorkspace` and `retry_on_pending_write()` (finding 6). Split it:

```rust
pub struct Workspace { /* owns mutable state; !Clone */ }

impl Workspace {
    pub fn open(opts: WorkspaceOptions) -> Result<Self>;
    pub fn open_scoped(opts: WorkspaceOptions, seeds: &[Utf8PathBuf], hops: u8) -> Result<Self>;
    pub fn snapshot(&self) -> Snapshot;              // O(1) Arc clone, Send + Sync + 'static
    pub fn apply_change(&mut self, change: Change) -> Result<ChangeSummary>;
    pub fn flush_cache(&self) -> Result<CacheStats>;
    pub fn fingerprint(&self) -> WorkspaceFingerprint;
    pub fn analysis_host(&self) -> &AnalysisCache;   // named escape hatch, cf. raw_database()
}

#[derive(Clone)]
pub struct Snapshot { index: Arc<WorkspaceIndex>, cache: Arc<AnalysisCache>, fp: WorkspaceFingerprint }
```

`&mut self` on `apply_change` and `&self` on `snapshot` is the entire concurrency design, checked at compile time. Then add inherent forwarding methods on `Workspace` (`ws.search(&opts)` ≡ `ws.snapshot().search(&opts)`) so the snapshot is not ceremony for the 90% single-query case. Free functions stay as one-shot wrappers: `pub fn search(o: &SearchOptions) -> Result<SearchResponse> { Workspace::open(o.into())?.search(o) }`.

"A daemon is a long-lived `Workspace`" is correct and is what finding 5 demonstrates in the opposite direction — ty's daemon-less CLI is a *short-lived* `ProjectDatabase` with the incremental machinery deliberately disabled (`disable_lru`, `freeze`). Give `WorkspaceOptions` a `Lifetime::{OneShot, Session}` hint that does the same thing: `OneShot` skips maintaining anything needed only for invalidation.

**Proposal 5 — `ws.invalidate(&changed_paths)`: refine to `apply_change(Change)`.**

Path-only invalidation is strictly less expressive than rust-analyzer's `Vec<(FileId, Option<String>)>` (finding 7) and Monokl needs the extra expressiveness the moment Wisp or an editor has an unsaved buffer. Take a transactional value:

```rust
pub struct Change { files: Vec<(Utf8PathBuf, FileContent)>, opts: Option<WorkspaceOptions> }
pub enum FileContent { Reread, Text(String), Deleted }

impl Change {
    pub fn touched<I: IntoIterator<Item = Utf8PathBuf>>(paths: I) -> Self;  // all FileContent::Reread
    pub fn set_text(&mut self, path: Utf8PathBuf, text: String);
    pub fn deleted(&mut self, path: Utf8PathBuf);
}
```

`Change::touched(git_delta)` gives you proposal 5's ergonomics verbatim, so nothing is lost. One transaction, one fingerprint bump, one re-fold of the enrichers — not N. Keep `invalidate` only if you want it as a documented alias for `apply_change(Change::touched(paths))`; do not make it the primitive. Also carry `opts` in the `Change`: rust-analyzer bundles `crate_graph` into `FileChange` precisely because a config change and a file change must be able to land atomically, and Monokl's `config_hash` (tsconfig) has the same property.

**Proposal 6 — public raw `Arc<FileAnalysis>` access: confirm, with two constraints.**

Direct precedent: `AnalysisHost::raw_database()` is public (finding 2). Constraints from the same source: (a) put the uncapped accessor on the *snapshot*, returning `Option<Arc<FileAnalysis>>` — not on a separate "raw API" surface that duplicates the query set; (b) the *default* query surface stays POD and budgeted, per `architecture.md:208-212`. Signature: `pub fn analysis(&self, path: &Utf8Path) -> Option<Arc<FileAnalysis>>` on `Snapshot`, plus `pub fn analyses(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = (&Utf8Path, &Arc<FileAnalysis>)>`. Document it as "no token budget, no truncation marker, no stability guarantee across minor versions" — that last clause is what buys you the freedom to reshape `FileAnalysis` without a semver major, and it is exactly the deal `raw_database()` makes.

**Proposal 7 — explicit `ws.flush_cache()`: confirm, unreservedly.**

Finding 18 gives you both halves: the std-library idiom says an implicit flush that swallows errors is a bug, and Monokl's `WorkspaceIndex::build` currently ends with `persist::flush(root, config_hash)?` where a caller cannot decline it. Refinement: make it `&self` (the `DashMap` gives interior mutability, and a snapshot-holding reader flushing the parse cache is harmless), return `Result<CacheStats>` so a caller can log what was written, and additionally flush from `Drop` on a best-effort basis with the errors logged at `warn!` — the `BufWriter` contract exactly.

**Proposal 10 (where it touches this track) — the benchmark should measure the session, not the batch.**

The workload that decides this design is not "open + 10-op batch" but "open once, then N changes each followed by a query." Add a `warm_after_change` group: open on 20k files, `apply_change(Change::touched(&[one_path]))`, re-query, and report the delta against a cold `Workspace::open`. That is the only number that tells you whether the session object earns its existence over the current free functions; the cold-vs-warm open comparison you already proposed only measures the disk cache, which exists today.

## Answers to the specific questions

**Constructor.** `Workspace::open(opts: WorkspaceOptions) -> Result<Workspace>`, with `WorkspaceOptions` gaining `lifetime: Lifetime`, `scope: Scope`, and the existing `root`/`tsconfig`. Do not use `new()` — `open` signals the fallible I/O. `open_scoped(opts, seeds, hops)` is better expressed as `Scope::Seeds { seeds, hops }` inside `WorkspaceOptions` than as a second constructor, so that a scoped and an unscoped workspace are the same type and `Provenance` can record which one answered.

**Snapshot type.** `Snapshot { index: Arc<WorkspaceIndex>, cache: Arc<AnalysisCache>, fp: WorkspaceFingerprint }`. `Clone`, `Send`, `Sync`, `'static`. No lifetime parameter tied to `&Workspace` — that would make the useful case (hand a snapshot to a rayon worker or a tokio task) impossible, and finding 5 shows ty doing exactly the `db.clone()` → `rayon::spawn(move || …)` move. Notably `Snapshot` should **not** derive `Serialize`.

**How a change enters.** `apply_change(&mut self, Change) -> Result<ChangeSummary>`, per proposal 5's verdict above. `ChangeSummary` reports which files were re-analyzed, which were cache hits, and the new fingerprint — so a caller can decide whether to re-run a query at all.

**`&self` on a snapshot, or `&Workspace`?** Both, deliberately. Queries are defined on `Snapshot` taking `&self`; `Workspace` gets thin forwarding inherent methods. Reason: defining them only on `Workspace` (Biome's choice) forces every query to take `&self` on a type that also has `&mut self` methods, which means either interior mutability with runtime retry (`retry_on_pending_write`, finding 6) or a lock. Defining them only on `Snapshot` makes the common one-query case a two-step dance. Forwarding methods cost one line each and are how `AnalysisHost` would work if rust-analyzer's callers were not all long-lived.

**Cancellation: no.** This is the sharpest recommendation in the report and it is a deliberate divergence from rust-analyzer. rust-analyzer cancels because Salsa's memo table is mutable storage shared by every outstanding snapshot, so a write must wait for readers to die (findings 3, 4). If `Snapshot` holds `Arc<WorkspaceIndex>` over an index that is never mutated after construction (finding 14), a write to `Workspace` builds a *new* `Arc<WorkspaceIndex>` and swaps it; existing snapshots remain internally consistent, merely stale. Stale is the condition proposal 4's `ws.is_current(&provenance)` already exists to detect — so the fingerprint mechanism you proposed is the correct and sufficient replacement for cancellation. Concretely, this buys: no `panic::catch_unwind`, no `UnwindSafe` bounds (finding 19), no `Cancellable<T>` in every signature, no `RefUnwindSafe` on `WorkspaceOptions`, no requirement that the host process enable unwinding (`panic = "abort"` stays viable). Revisit only if a `PrecisionUpgrader` (`06-daemon-architecture.md` §2) ever holds a genuinely shared mutable backend; even then, scope cancellation to that upgrader's own `Result`, not to the whole query API.

**Where serialization belongs.** Not on `Snapshot`, and not on the types reachable from `Snapshot`'s query methods. Findings 11–13 make this concrete: Monokl currently has one type set serving the public API, the disk cache format, and the agent JSON wire shape, which is three compatibility clocks on one struct. Split into three, in decreasing order of how much I would fight for it:

1. **Agent JSON output → `orin-contracts` (proposal 9), with hand-written `From<&monokl::X>` conversions.** This is the rust-analyzer rule applied literally, and `rust-project.json` is the worked precedent ("it doesn't include `CrateGraph` as is"). It is also what makes proposal 9's "pinned artifact JSON schemas" meaningful — a schema pinned against a type that is also the internal API is not pinned.
2. **Disk cache (`.monokl/cache.json`) → its own `persist::v1::*` types.** The version- and config-hash gate already in the spec makes a *breaking* change safe, but it does not stop a *silent* one: adding `#[serde(default)]` to a public API field changes the cache format's meaning without changing the version. Own types make that impossible.
3. **The `ide`-level types keep `Serialize` only if you accept that the public API is a wire format.** If step 1 lands, drop the derives. If it does not, at minimum move the presentation attributes (`skip_serializing_if`, `rename_all = "camelCase"`) off the analysis types — a `camelCase` rename on `SymbolEntry` is a JS-output decision leaking into a Rust struct that Wisp will consume in-process and never serialize.

Keep the `ide` shape rule regardless (finding 12): POD structs, public fields, offsets and strings rather than opaque handles. Monokl already satisfies this.

**Raw facts vs. budgeted agent output.** Precedent is strong and multiple: `grep-searcher`/`grep-printer` inside Monokl's own dependency tree, `ide` (viewmodel) vs `hir`/`base_db` (facts) in rust-analyzer, and LSP's `completionItem/resolve` / `workspaceSymbol/resolve` deferral-by-capability on the wire (finding 16). The generalizable rule from all three: the raw layer must not know the budget exists. Concretely, `budget::apply_budget` should be the last thing a `query()` does, operating on a fully-built `Vec<RankedBlock>`, and `Snapshot::analysis()` should not route through it at all. Monokl's stage-8 design already matches; the risk is drift, and the way to prevent drift is a type: make the budgeted path return `Budgeted<T> { value: T, truncation: Option<Truncation> }` so that "I forgot to record the truncation" is a compile error rather than a missing field.

## Recommendations not on the list

**R1. Add `Snapshot::is_current(&self) -> bool` alongside proposal 4's `ws.is_current(&provenance)`.** Once snapshots are cheap and long-lived, the common question is not "is this provenance record still valid" but "is the snapshot I am holding still the newest one." One `WorkspaceFingerprint` comparison. It is also what makes cancellation-free operation legible to a caller: they can check, rather than being panicked at.

**R2. Make `WorkspaceIndex` construction lazy per-enricher.** Finding 9 — "it's not the incrementality that makes an IDE fast. Rather, it's laziness." `dependents` needs only the import graph; `symbols` needs neither the import graph nor the symbol index (it analyzes the given files directly, per spec §20). Today `WorkspaceIndex::build` runs both enrichers unconditionally over the whole tree. `Snapshot::import_graph()` / `symbol_index()` returning `&ImportGraph` from a `OnceLock` inside the `Arc` costs nothing and skips a full fold for the majority of queries. This is orthogonal to proposal 3's scoped open and composes with it.

**R3. Adopt durability tiers now, at the fingerprint level, without adopting Salsa.** Finding 8: rust-analyzer's tiers are assigned by *provenance* (library vs. local), not measured. Monokl has the same free signal — `node_modules/`, vendored directories, and anything outside the Git working tree change on a different clock than `src/`. Make `WorkspaceFingerprint` a pair `(durable: u64, volatile: u64)` rather than one hash. Then `ws.is_current(&provenance)` for a result derived only from durable inputs stays true across an ordinary edit, and `apply_change` on a `src/` file does not invalidate cached answers about vendored code. This is the cheap 90% of durability's benefit with none of Salsa's machinery, and it makes the eventual Salsa migration (`PRINCIPLES.md` open track) a narrowing rather than a rewrite.

**R4. Give `QueryResponse` (proposal 2) a per-op `Provenance`, not one per response.** This is proposal 8's argument (per-edge precision) applied one level up, and it follows from batching: a 10-op batch spanning `search` (Exact, TS) and `refs` (Structural, Rust) has no single honest precision. Batching without per-op provenance would silently flatten what proposal 4 exists to preserve.

**R5. Do not put `Send + Sync + RefUnwindSafe` on `Workspace` — put it on `Snapshot`.** Biome bounds its `Workspace` trait `Send + Sync + RefUnwindSafe` because the workspace itself is shared across LSP request threads. If snapshots are the shared thing, `Workspace` needs no bounds at all, which keeps `Box<dyn LanguageAnalyzer>` and any future `PrecisionUpgrader` holding a subprocess handle out of a `Sync` straitjacket. `06-daemon-architecture.md` §3 already requires `PrecisionUpgrader: Send + Sync`; that requirement gets *weaker*, not stronger, under a snapshot design, because the upgrader can be owned by `Workspace` and consulted only during `apply_change`.

**R6. Name the escape hatch after what it costs.** `raw_database()` works for rust-analyzer because "database" already reads as internal. `ws.analysis(path)` reads like the primary API. Prefer `Snapshot::file_analysis_unbudgeted(path)` or keep `analysis()` but gate the module behind a non-default `raw-api` cargo feature, so that a downstream crate depending on it is visible in `Cargo.toml` rather than discovered at the next semver bump.

## Contradictions and open questions

**C1. Biome and rust-analyzer disagree, and the disagreement is about the transport, not about sessions.** Biome's `&self`-everywhere, params-struct-everywhere `Workspace` exists because it is pre-shaped for a `WorkspaceClient` speaking over a transport (finding 6). rust-analyzer explicitly refuses that pre-shaping — "`ide` crate strives to provide a *perfect* API. Although at the moment it has only one consumer, the LSP server, LSP *does not* influence its API design." If Monokl ever wants an out-of-process daemon that Wisp talks to over a socket, Biome's shape is the cheaper path; if the daemon is always in-process (Wisp embedding Monokl as a library, per `00-context.md`), rust-analyzer's is strictly better. The stated plan is in-process. I recommend rust-analyzer's shape, but this is the one verdict that would flip on a change of that assumption.

**C2. Salsa's `StorageHandle` may make the snapshot question moot later, and I could not determine its exact contract.** `docs.rs/salsa` lists `StorageHandle` as "a handle to non-local database state" alongside `Storage` ("with local state that can be used to drive computations"), which reads like a `Send` snapshot handle designed for exactly this. The salsa book's cancellation page is a 404 (`salsa-rs.github.io/salsa/reference/cancellation.html`), and I could not find its replacement, so I could not verify whether `StorageHandle` avoids the "write waits for readers" behaviour of finding 4 or merely relocates it. If Monokl ever adopts Salsa, this is the first thing to check.

**C3. Whether stale snapshots leak memory in practice is unmeasured.** The cancellation-free design (verdict above) means a caller holding a snapshot pins an `Arc<WorkspaceIndex>` and every `Arc<FileAnalysis>` it references. Because `FileAnalysis` is shared with the live cache by content hash, the marginal cost of one stale snapshot should be the index only (`ARCHITECTURE.md` estimates the whole `WorkspaceIndex` at 90–140MB at 50k files, which is not marginal). rust-analyzer sidesteps this because Salsa's LRU bounds the memo table; ty sidesteps it by disabling the LRU precisely when it knows there will be no second revision (finding 5). Monokl has no such bound. Proposal 10's benchmark should hold two snapshots across a change and measure RSS.

**C4. The gopls citation in `06-daemon-architecture.md` §3 does not check out against the document class it implies (finding 20).** The claim is probably true of gopls' implementation but is not in `gopls/doc/design/design.md`. Either re-source it to `golang/tools/gopls/internal/cache` or soften it.

**C5. No evidence found either way on whether `open_scoped` (proposal 3) can produce an honest `Provenance`.** A seed-plus-N-hops closure means `dependents(f)` is answered against a partial import graph, and the answer "3 dependents" is indistinguishable from "3 dependents that happen to be inside the closure." rust-analyzer has no analogue — its crate graph is always complete — and I found no precedent in ty, Biome, or gopls for a deliberately partial index. Either `Scope::Seeds` must downgrade the precision of every graph-derived operation to `Heuristic`, or `DependentsResult` needs a "boundary reached" marker distinct from the existing truncation marker. This is a real gap in proposal 3 and it is a correctness issue, not an ergonomics one.
