- https://docs.rs/salsa/latest/salsa/ and salsa overview — likely (per-field dependency tracking, early cutoff, durability)
- Searches for a published SQLite-vs-in-memory crossover for code intelligence, and for `zoekt` seconds-per-GB index throughput — **no primary source found**; see Contradictions.

## Findings

1. **Glean's incrementality is fact-ownership, not file-diffing, and its unit of ownership is arbitrary.** "A unit is just a string; Glean doesn't impose any particular meaning on units so the indexer can use whatever convention it likes, but typically a unit might be a filename or module name." Units are never declared — "a unit exists if it is the owner of at least one fact" — and get a `UnitId` assigned by the storage backend on first sight. Facts are owned by *ownership sets* with the grammar `set ::= unit | set_1 || ... || set_n | set_1 && ... && set_n`, each interned as a `UsetId`. The scheme's efficiency rests on an explicit assumption Wisp should note: "typically 10-100x more facts than sets."

2. **Glean's soundness invariant is exactly the one a scoped/partial index has to satisfy, and it is stated formally.** "In a DB consisting of all the visible facts for a given set of excluded units, every fact referenced by a visible fact is also visible." Maintaining it requires *widening* ownership rather than narrowing it: for fact F (owner A) referencing fact G (owner B), G's owner becomes `A || B`. Derived facts invert the connective: "A derived fact should be visible if and only if all the facts that it was derived from are visible" — owner `O1 && ... && On`. Cost of computing all this: "2-3% for Python, for Hack it was in the noise," with query overhead under 10%. Glean also documents an unfixed hole: "Incremental derivation on stacked databases isn't yet implemented" to repair downstream ownership. Meta's framing of *why*: "we can't provide up-to-date information about the latest code because indexing the entire repository can take a long time. The index is perpetually out of date, perhaps by many hours" — the goal is O(changes), not O(repository).

3. **rust-analyzer's VFS is the canonical `apply_change(ChangeSet)` design, and it is content-hash-gated at the event source.** `pub struct ChangedFile { pub file_id: FileId, pub change: Change }` with `pub enum Change { Create(Vec<u8>, u64), Modify(Vec<u8>, u64), Delete }` — the `u64` is a content hash (`hash_once::<FxHasher>(&*v)`), and a set whose hash matches the existing one **records no change at all**. `take_changes()` "drains and returns all the changes in the `Vfs`". `GlobalState::process_changes` then takes the whole drained batch, folds every entry into a single `ChangeWithProcMacros`, and applies it once: `let cancellation_time = self.analysis_host.apply_change(change);`. Crucially it distinguishes structural from content changes — `if has_structure_changes { let roots = self.source_root_config.partition(vfs); change.set_roots(roots); }` — because creates and deletes repartition source roots while modifies do not. `apply_change` returning a cancellation time is Salsa cancelling every in-flight query against that database, which is why Monokl's own daemon spec (§3) already mandates a single-threaded prime phase before parallel readers.

4. **Salsa's durability tier is the cheap generalisation of "which changes can I ignore".** rust-analyzer's own writeup: "any change to `src/lib.rs` necessitates checking all the queries related to standard library (which adds up to about 300ms)." The fix is not finer-grained deps but a *version vector* — inputs get a durability (volatile/normal/durable), derived queries take the minimum of their inputs, and a revision bump only touches the components matching the changed inputs, letting Salsa "skip over the entire query subgraph" unvalidated. This is a strictly cheaper win than a full Salsa adoption and is available to Monokl without one.

5. **moon/Nx/Turborepo all implement the identical three-step "git delta → seed set → closure", and the interesting variation is in what they record and how far they walk.** Nx: "Use Git to determine the files you changed in your PR" → map to owning projects via the project graph → "use the project graph to determine which projects depend on the projects you modified"; `.gitignore`/`.nxignore` globs are excluded; a lockfile change marks *all* projects affected by default, tunable via `projectsAffectedByDependencyUpdates: "auto"`. moon: touched files come from the VCS (local working changes, or `HEAD` vs `vcs.defaultBranch` for `--remote`), filterable by `--status` (`added`/`deleted`/`modified`/`staged`/`unstaged`/`untracked`), then intersected against each task's declared `inputs` — moon "exit[s] early if no files intersect with the task's inputs". Closure depth is a dial, not a boolean: `--upstream` and `--downstream` each take `none` (default) / `direct` / `deep`, and `moon query affected` returns `{ projects: Record<Id, AffectedState>, tasks: Record<Target, AffectedState> }`. Turborepo's SCM filter is `--filter=[HEAD^1]` / `[main...my-feature]` / `[sha...sha]`, and notably its dependents/dependencies microsyntax (`...pkg`, `pkg...`) is documented *separately* from the SCM filter — i.e. "changed" and "closure of changed" are deliberately different operators.

6. **moon v1.29 records *why* something is affected, and that is the piece Wisp actually needs.** Affected state is attributed to one or more of: touched files, environment variables, upstream dependencies, downstream dependents, internal logic — persisted to `.moon/cache/runReport.json` under `context.affected`. moon's own release framing is that this exists to "answer the 'why'". A Wisp `impact` result that says "SPEC-021 is affected" without saying "because `src/retry/policy.rs` is in its plan's declared files, and that file is modified-unstaged" is strictly worse than moon's, and Wisp's provenance rule already demands the stronger form.

7. **Bazel and Nix are the two canonical "content hash is the key, mtime is a hint" designs, and Monokl already implements Bazel's exact shape.** Bazel's action cache key is "declared inputs, output filenames, command line, and environment variables" with only `--action_env`-whitelisted env included; mtime appears nowhere in the key. But at the *file* layer Bazel keeps "a bounded-size cache in memory of (path, inode, mtime, size) -> MD5", recomputing a checksum only when mtime moved. That is character-for-character Monokl's documented 4-tier lookup (`stat → persist::lookup(mtime+size) → read + blake3 → in-memory (verify hash) → persist::lookup_by_hash + refresh_mtime → parse`). Nix goes further and makes content the *identity*: a content-addressed store path's "digest of the store path is solely computed from the file system object graph...references...store directory [and] name of the store object, and not any other information," so "store invalidation occurs only when actual content changes, not when build configurations shift."

8. **Bazel's `--watchfs` is the cautionary tale for anyone tempted to make a file watcher load-bearing.** It genuinely helps: with it Bazel can "avoid even calling `stat` on all the input files because it knows which ones changed." But: "That doesn't help on the first build after the server process is started because it still needs to re-checksum all the files"; it is a startup option, so toggling it restarts the server and re-parses all BUILD files; and it has repeatedly shipped bugs where the watcher "disregards `.bazelignore` and WORKSPACE file exclusions and scans folders anyway", with Windows startup reported up to 1.5 minutes on workspaces containing large irrelevant subtrees. A watcher is a latency optimisation over a correct stat/hash path, never a substitute for one.

9. **tree-sitter's incremental reparse requires holding the previous `Tree` and feeding it edits, which a batch process structurally cannot do — but a Wisp daemon can.** The API is two-step: `ts_tree_edit()` with a `TSInputEdit { start_byte, start_point, old_end_byte, old_end_point, new_end_byte, new_end_point }`, then `ts_parser_parse()` passing the old tree, which "will create a new tree that internally shares structure with the old tree". Monokl §11 correctly concludes this is irrelevant to a fresh-process-per-invocation CLI and budgets every tree-sitter language at cold-parse cost. That conclusion is scoped to the *current* architecture and stops holding the moment proposal 1's long-lived `Workspace` exists inside a Wisp service — at which point Monokl would be holding the previous tree and discarding it. Monokl's own §11 also records the floor: a 1.6MB JSON file takes ~1.2s cold and **~0.7s to reparse with zero edits** — incremental is not free even at its best.

10. **CodeGraph is the closest shipped analogue and gives real incremental numbers; GitNexus and GitLab's KG do not.** CodeGraph stores a SQLite DB with FTS5 at `.codegraph/codegraph.db`, kept current by three layers: a native FSEvents/inotify/ReadDirectoryChangesW watcher with a 2000ms debounce (`CODEGRAPH_WATCH_DEBOUNCE_MS`, clamped 100ms–60s) so bursts collapse into one sync; staleness banners prepended to MCP responses during the debounce window telling the agent to read the file directly; and a connect-time reconciliation doing size + mtime + content-hash checks against the working tree to catch offline edits. Numbers: single-file resync ~0.3s on a 4,400-file project; cold index of the 27k-file Swift compiler repo ~100s; Linux kernel (70k files) under 12 min on a 2-core/6GB VPS. It claims 62% fewer tokens / 44% cheaper across seven benchmark repos versus file-reading — but Monokl §2 already records that codegraph's published cost-savings claim reversed under independent replication when the cached/fresh token mix shifted, so treat that pair of numbers as unreliable while treating the latency numbers as plausible. GitNexus is not a comparable data point: it is browser/client-side, uses LadybugDB rather than SQLite, and incremental indexing was still on its roadmap as of mid-2026. GitLab's Knowledge Graph is a caution rather than a precedent — it was built on KùzuDB, "an embedded graph database chosen for its performance", which "has been archived, rendering it an unviable foundation for a production system and necessitating a new graph database selection."

11. **Per-artifact Git subprocess calls cost ~8ms each as a floor, measured on the smallest possible repository.** In `/Users/gabe/Projects/wisp` (6 tracked files, so essentially zero real work): 50 × `git status --porcelain` = 442ms (**8.8ms/call**); 50 × `git log -1 --format=%H -- README.md` = 363ms (**7.3ms/call**); one batched `git log -50 --name-only --format=%H` = **12ms total**. That ~8ms is process spawn plus repository discovery, independent of repo size — on a real repository `git status` adds actual index/worktree scanning on top. A 50-artifact workspace doing one status and one log per artifact pays ≈800ms of pure overhead before any Wisp work happens; the batched equivalent is ~20ms. The saving is roughly 40×, and it grows with artifact count while the batched cost stays flat.

12. **`gix-status` is explicitly not production-grade, and gitoxide says so in its own status table.** Only `gix-lock` (Tier 1) and `gix-tempfile` (Tier 2) are listed as production-ready; `gix` itself is "Initial Development" with "rough but complete docs, possibly incomplete functionality", and `gix-status` is "usable but incomplete" and is *not* among the stabilization candidates. Functionally it does cover the needed cases — "differences between index and worktree to turn index into worktree" with rename tracking and untracked files, and index-to-index diffing — but explicitly lacks "support for fs-monitor for modification checks" and "sparse-index and split-index aware status acceleration". The API surface exists (`Repository::status()`, `index_worktree_status()`, `tree_index_status()`, `is_dirty()`). No published `gix status` vs `git status` benchmark was found; the "dramatically faster than C Git" claims in secondary write-ups are not backed by anything in the repository itself.

13. **Scoped analysis has real precedent, and in every case the reverse-closure query is the one that breaks.** Kythe's `CompilationUnit`/`.kzip` is per-compilation-unit extraction done properly: the unit is self-contained *together with the content of all the source files and other inputs the compiler needs* (headers, dependency type snapshots) — i.e. the forward closure is bundled, not assumed present — and cross-references are only produced by a later global merge across units. TypeScript project references scope compilation the same way: `composite: true` forces `declaration: true` and requires every implementation file be explicitly matched, importing a referenced project loads its `.d.ts` rather than its source, and the boundary is documented as one-way — "Referenced projects don't 'know' who depends on them", "Find All References is limited to single projects", with `declarationMap: true` buying go-to-definition across the boundary and nothing else. `cargo check -p` checks the named package and its dependencies, never its dependents. Sourcegraph's fast always-available tier is the same trade in a different dimension: search-based navigation "can occasionally return false-positive and false-negative results", is worse "for tokens with common names (such as `Get`)", and "is limited to returning definitions and references within a single repository" — precise/SCIP is what you need "if you require 100% confidence in accuracy for a definition or reference results".

14. **Monokl's `FileIdx` is positional over the sorted analysed file set, which makes both scoped open and cheap invalidation harder than they look.** `WorkspaceIndex::build` sorts analyses by `source_path`, then assigns `FileIdx(i as u32)` by enumeration position. `ImportGraph` stores `reverse: FxHashMap<FileIdx, Vec<FileIdx>>` and `SymbolIndex` keys on `FileIdx` too. Two consequences neither proposal 3 nor 5 currently accounts for. (a) Adding or deleting any file renumbers every `FileIdx` after it, so a create/delete invalidates the entire `ImportGraph` and `SymbolIndex`, while a pure content modification of an existing file does not — the same structural-vs-content split rust-analyzer encodes as `has_structure_changes`, but Monokl has no equivalent guard. (b) `FileIdx` for the same path differs between a scoped open and a full open, so no identity built on `FileIdx` (proposal 4's `SymbolId` included) can be compared across the two. Separately, `ImportGraph.reverse` is populated only from edges observed during the whole-tree pass, so under a scoped open `dependents_of` returns a silent under-approximation with no marker — it cannot distinguish "no dependents" from "no dependents inside the scope".

15. **`WorkspaceIndex::build` brackets its work with `persist::init(root, config_hash)?` on entry and `persist::flush(root, config_hash)?` on exit, which is the concrete defect proposal 7 names.** With free functions like `pipeline::dependents(file, root)` each calling `build_standard` internally, a 10-op batch is 10 index builds and 10 disk-cache flushes of the same data. Both Bazel (action cache write is a distinct step from action execution) and Glean (a DB is *completed* and becomes immutable, separately from being written into) separate compute from cache commit. The `persist` layer already carries a `queue_write`/`flush` split internally — the API just never exposes the seam.

16. **Monokl's own latency targets are the numbers proposal 12's deferral rests on, and they are asserted, not measured.** Spec line 3135: "Latency targets at 50k files: symbols(1 file) cold <50ms / warm <5ms / lite <5ms; dependents cold <15s / warm <30ms / lite <50ms; search(3-term) cold <15s / warm <300ms; WorkspaceIndex::build <15s cold; disk cache flush <800ms." §4 separately estimates the warm in-memory refold at "100-500ms at 10k files and 300ms-1.5s at 50k". Spec line 3150 confirms all four criterion groups in `benches/pipeline.rs` are "empty stubs", and §11 explicitly warns the 15s cold-build target should read as "unvalidated and plausibly optimistic". Every claim about where the persistent-index crossover sits currently traces back to these unmeasured numbers.

## Verdict on proposed changes

**3 — Scoped open (`Workspace::open_scoped(root, seeds, hops)`): refine, substantially.** The idea is sound and well-precedented (finding 13), but "same `Workspace` type, fewer files" is the wrong shape and will produce silently wrong `dependents`/`refs` answers (finding 14). Three concrete refinements. (a) Make completeness a first-class axis orthogonal to `CapabilityPrecision`: every result carries `scope: Complete | Partial { seeds, hops, analysed_files }`. Precision answers "how well was this resolved"; completeness answers "over what file set" — Sourcegraph's search-based tier is imprecise-but-whole-tree, a scoped open is precise-but-partial, and one enum cannot carry both. (b) Reverse-closure operations must not silently degrade. `dependents`/`refs` under `Partial` scope should return `Unsupported` with a `Diagnostic` naming the whole-tree operation the caller needs, exactly as TypeScript makes Find-All-References a non-feature across project boundaries rather than a lossy one. Forward-closure operations — `symbols`, `definition`, `explain`, and `search` restricted to the scoped file set — are sound, provided the closure is genuinely materialised the way Kythe bundles required inputs, not merely assumed. (c) `hops` needs an explicit unresolved-import outcome: an import that resolves to a path outside the scope is a real event that must surface as a diagnostic, not as a missing edge. Consider naming it `ScopedWorkspace` (a distinct type exposing only the sound operations) rather than an option on `Workspace` — the type system should carry this, not documentation.

**5 — Git-delta-driven invalidation (`ws.invalidate(&changed_paths)`): refine → `ws.apply_change(ChangeSet)`.** The direction is right and matches every system surveyed, but a bare path list is the wrong payload. Adopt rust-analyzer's shape (finding 3): `ChangeSet { files: Vec<ChangedFile> }` with `Change::{Create(bytes, hash), Modify(bytes, hash), Delete}`, applied as one batch, not one call per path. Four reasons. (a) The caller already read the bytes — Wisp will have run one `git status`/`git diff` and, for small artifacts, already have the content; a path-only API forces Monokl to re-stat and re-read what the caller just had, and Bazel's `--watchfs` lesson (finding 8) is that knowing *which* files changed is the expensive part, which the caller here already solved. (b) Content-hash gating belongs at the event source: rust-analyzer records *no change* when the new hash equals the old, which is what stops a `touch` or a save-with-no-edit from cascading. (c) Create/Delete must be distinguishable from Modify, because in Monokl they are categorically more expensive — they renumber `FileIdx` and invalidate both enrichers (finding 14). Mirror `has_structure_changes`: a `ChangeSet` of pure `Modify`s can re-run only the affected files' analyses and patch the enrichers; any `Create`/`Delete` triggers a rebuild until `FileIdx` stops being positional. (d) Batching lets one truncation/diagnostic record cover the whole change, matching proposal 2. "Just re-stat" is *also* correct and should remain the default for `Workspace::open` — Monokl's 4-tier lookup is already Bazel's design (finding 7) and needs no help; `apply_change` is the optimisation for a long-lived `Workspace` where the caller has better information than a stat loop, not a replacement for it.

**7 — Explicit `ws.flush_cache()`: confirm.** Grounded directly in the spec's own code (finding 15) — `build` calls `persist::init`/`persist::flush`, so an N-op batch flushes N times. Two additions: flush must be idempotent and cheap when nothing is queued (so callers can flush defensively), and a `Workspace` should flush on `Drop` unless explicitly flushed, so the ergonomic path stays correct for callers who forget. Note the existing `flush()` already documents a poisoned-lock hazard where the queue may be "drained by `flush()` but not yet re-committed" — exposing flush publicly widens that window and needs the failure to stay propagated, not swallowed.

**10 — Briefing-workload benchmark on 5k/20k/50k fixtures, cold vs. warm: confirm, and extend.** This is the highest-value item in my scope, because finding 16 shows *every* architectural decision here — including proposal 12's — currently rests on unmeasured assertions in a spec whose own research log flags them as "plausibly optimistic". Three extensions. (a) Add a third condition beyond cold/warm: **incremental** — open, `apply_change` a 1-file / 10-file / 100-file delta, re-run the batch. That is the actual Wisp daemon workload and no current benchmark group covers it. (b) Report `Create`/`Delete` deltas separately from `Modify` deltas; finding 14 predicts a step change between them, and if the benchmark averages them the `FileIdx` problem stays invisible. (c) Report the enricher-refold cost separately from parse cost — §4's whole 50k-file argument is that refold is cheap relative to parse, and that split is precisely what the benchmark must confirm or kill.

**12 — Defer SQLite/FTS, in-memory refold from JSON: confirm, with one carve-out.** The numbers support this more strongly than the proposal claims, because the relevant scale is not code-repo scale. Every persistent-index data point found is about *code* files at scale — CodeGraph reaches for SQLite at 4.4k–70k source files (finding 10), Glean at Meta-monorepo scale (finding 2), Monokl's own threshold estimate is 50k source files (finding 16). Wisp's artifact graph is bounded by human authorship rate: specs, plans, requirements, arch models — tens to low hundreds of JSON documents, single-digit megabytes total. Refolding that in memory is milliseconds; there is no measured or plausible argument for SQLite at that scale, and D-004's own rebuildability requirement plus Milestone 2's "delete `.wisp/` then rebuilding produces the same derived graph" gate mean the refold path has to work correctly regardless, so SQLite would be a second implementation of something already required. The carve-out: `.wisp/` currently bundles three unrelated things under one storage decision — (a) the artifact/link graph, which should be an in-memory refold and needs nothing on disk; (b) the brief cache, which is a pure key→blob store and is better served by content-addressed files under `.wisp/cache/briefs/<key>` than by a database, giving atomic writes and trivial eviction for free; (c) FTS over prose docs and ADRs, which is the *only* part with a genuine scale question, since a repo's `docs/` tree is not bounded by artifact count. Defer (a) and (b) indefinitely; keep (c) as the single measured trigger for adopting SQLite, and say so in D-004 rather than deferring the whole store as one undifferentiated decision. Corollary: the Milestone 2 acceptance gates ("editing a spec marks linked plans/briefs stale"; "editing an unrelated file does not invalidate an unrelated briefing") are storage-agnostic and should be written against the invalidation contract, not against SQLite.

**15 — Batch Git calls (one `git status` per workspace, or `gix`): confirm the batching, refine the `gix` half.** Batching is confirmed by direct measurement — ~8ms per subprocess floor, ~40× saving at 50 artifacts, and the batched cost is flat in artifact count (finding 11). This is not an optimisation, it is the difference between sub-100ms and near-second latency on the artifact-only path. But "or `gix`" conflates two independent decisions. `gix`'s mature surface (object/ref/commit/tree reads, revision walking, diffing) is exactly what Wisp's HEAD/tree fingerprints and commit-distance freshness (proposal 13) need, and using it there is right. `gix-status` specifically is "Initial Development", is not a stabilization candidate, and lacks fs-monitor and sparse/split-index acceleration (finding 12) — and worktree status is the one call in the hot path on every invocation. Recommendation: put VCS access behind a small trait with two implementations, use `gix` for object/ref reads from the start, and start worktree status on one batched `git status --porcelain=v2 -z --untracked-files=all` subprocess (~8ms plus real scan cost, one spawn per workspace, `-z` for unambiguous parsing of paths with spaces or unicode). Swap to `gix::Repository::index_worktree_status()` behind the trait once `gix-status` reaches a stabilization tier, with a benchmark to justify the switch rather than a stability claim. Also adopt moon's `--status` filter concept: Wisp needs to distinguish staged / unstaged / untracked / renamed, because Q-010's four freshness states ("clean matching commit, clean different commit, dirty but unaffected, dirty potentially affected") cannot be derived from a flat changed-path list.

## Recommendations not on the list

1. **Record *why* something is affected, per moon's `AffectedState`.** moon attributes each affected project to touched files / env vars / upstream / downstream / internal logic, and persists it to `runReport.json` (finding 6). Wisp's provenance rule demands this anyway; the cheap version is an `AffectedBy` enum on every `impact` result edge. Without it, `wisp impact` is a list of names an agent cannot audit.

2. **Make closure depth a dial, not a boolean.** Both moon (`--upstream`/`--downstream` × `none`/`direct`/`deep`) and Turborepo (`...pkg` / `pkg...`) treat "changed" and "closure of changed" as different operators. `wisp impact --paths X` should default to `direct` and expose `deep`, because an unbounded reverse closure on a monorepo returns everything and is useless as a briefing input. This also gives proposal 3's `hops` parameter a sibling with matching vocabulary.

3. **Adopt Nx's lockfile rule for Wisp's own global inputs.** Nx marks all projects affected when the lockfile changes. Wisp's equivalents — the pinned schema registry version, the Wisp config hash, the Monokl version/config hash — should each invalidate everything derived, and Wisp's own briefing cache key (already listed in `02-architecture-and-contracts.md`) correctly includes them. Make that a stated rule with a test, not an implicit consequence of key composition.

4. **Give Monokl Salsa's durability tiers without adopting Salsa.** Finding 4: rust-analyzer recovered ~300ms per keystroke purely by tagging inputs with a durability level. Monokl's equivalent partition is free and obvious — `node_modules`, `target`, vendored deps, and anything outside the git worktree are `Durable`; tracked workspace files are `Volatile`. A `ChangeSet` touching only volatile inputs can skip revalidating any cached analysis whose inputs are entirely durable. This is a small deterministic change, is orthogonal to the open Salsa investigation in §4, and would make proposal 5 meaningfully cheaper.

5. **Model Wisp's brief cache on Glean's ownership sets rather than a flat key.** Finding 2 gives the exact semantics for free: a brief is a *derived fact*, so it is valid iff **all** its inputs are valid — the `&&` connective. Storing a brief alongside the set of `(source, content_hash)` pairs it was derived from, and validating by intersection, is both cheaper and more explainable than a single opaque composite key, because on a miss you can report *which* input moved. That directly serves D-008's explainability requirement and Milestone 2's "editing an unrelated file does not invalidate an unrelated briefing" gate.

6. **Stop `FileIdx` from being positional before either proposal 3 or 5 is built.** Finding 14 is a prerequisite, not a detail: while `FileIdx` is an enumeration index over the sorted analysed set, scoped open produces incomparable identities and any create/delete forces a full rebuild. The minimal fix is to key `ImportGraph`/`SymbolIndex` on a stable id (interned path, or the `SymbolId` proposal 4 already wants) and keep `FileIdx` purely as a dense internal array offset that is never observable and never compared across builds. Proposal 4's `SymbolId` must be defined as path + qualified name + kind with no `FileIdx` component — which the proposal already says, but the reason is stronger than "lines move".

7. **Do not make a file watcher load-bearing for correctness.** Wisp's architecture doc already says `notify` is "service phase only, never required for correctness" — finding 8 is the evidence for keeping that line. CodeGraph's watcher design is worth copying in one specific respect though: its *staleness banner* during the debounce window, which tells the agent explicitly that a file is pending re-index and it should read directly. That is the same honesty discipline as Monokl's truncation marker and Wisp's provenance classes, applied to time rather than to budget.

8. **Adopt Kythe's "bundle the required inputs" discipline for any scoped mode.** A scoped open should record the exact set of files it analysed as part of its provenance, so `ws.is_current(&provenance)` (proposal 4) can answer "is this still valid" *and* "was this ever complete". A provenance that records a fingerprint but not a file set cannot distinguish a stale full analysis from a fresh partial one.

## Contradictions and open questions

1. **The ~50k-file crossover has no external corroboration.** Searches for published guidance on when a persistent code index beats in-memory re-derivation returned nothing usable, and no seconds-per-GB figure for zoekt index builds was findable. The available adjacent data points cut *against* a threshold that high: CodeGraph persists to SQLite at 4,400 files and claims benefit there; Sourcegraph and Glean persist at every scale. Nothing found says "below N files, don't persist." The 50k number appears to be Monokl-internal reasoning about *its own* refold cost, and finding 16 shows that reasoning rests on unmeasured targets. It should be described as an untested hypothesis with proposal 10 as the test, not as a threshold. Note this does not weaken proposal 12, which stands on a different and firmer argument (Wisp's artifact count is bounded by authorship, not by repo size).

2. **CodeGraph's own incremental numbers are internally inconsistent across sources.** The repository page reports ~0.4s resync for the 27k-file Swift compiler repo; the README as fetched reports "~4" seconds for the same repo and edit class. One of the two is wrong and I could not determine which. Both are consistent with "sub-second-to-few-seconds for a single-file edit at 27k files", which is the only claim worth carrying forward.

3. **Monokl's blanket "budget tree-sitter at cold-parse cost, full stop" is scoped to an architecture proposal 1 changes.** §11's reasoning — "monokl never holds a previous tree to diff against" — is correct today and false the moment a long-lived `Workspace` lives inside a Wisp service. That does not make the conclusion wrong now, but it should be annotated as conditional rather than absolute, since proposal 1 is on the same list.

4. **Glean documents an unrepaired hole in stacked-DB incremental derivation** ("Incremental derivation on stacked databases isn't yet implemented" to fix downstream fact ownership). The most sophisticated production system in this space has not fully solved incremental derivation over layered state. That is a reason for Wisp to keep its derived layer cheap enough to discard and recompute, rather than to build a layered invalidation scheme it would have to get more right than Meta has.

5. **No `gix status` vs `git status` benchmark exists in any primary source I could find.** The "dramatically faster than C Git for status" claims trace only to secondary write-ups; gitoxide's own repository makes no such claim. Proposal 15's `gix` half therefore cannot be justified on performance grounds today — only on "typed, in-process, no subprocess parsing", which is a real but different argument and is weakened by `gix-status`'s stated maturity.

6. **Whether a Wisp `ChangeSet` should carry file contents is genuinely open.** rust-analyzer carries `Vec<u8>` because the LSP client already sent the text. Wisp's git-status path knows paths but not necessarily contents, so carrying bytes would mean Wisp reads files purely to hand them to Monokl — plausibly slower than letting Monokl's own stat-gated cache decide. The honest shape may be `Change::Modify { path, content: Option<Vec<u8>> }`, with `None` meaning "re-stat it yourself". I found no precedent for the optional form; every system surveyed sits at one extreme or the other.

7. **Nothing found addresses how to invalidate a *derived cross-domain* record like a Wisp brief when its inputs span two independently-cached systems** (Monokl's content hashes and Git's commit state). Glean's ownership sets are the closest model (finding 2 / recommendation 5) but assume one fact store. The `WorkspaceFingerprint` + `is_current(&provenance)` pair in proposal 4 is the right primitive; whether it is *sufficient* — specifically whether Monokl can answer `is_current` without rebuilding the index — is not settled by any source I read and should be an explicit acceptance criterion on proposal 4.

31	1. **LSP forbids JSON-RPC batching outright, in normative language.** Base Protocol 0.9 §"Base Protocol", line 122: *"The base protocol uses request, response, and notification objects as specified in the JSON-RPC protocol. It currently does not support JSON-RPC batch messages; protocol clients and servers must not send JSON-RPC requests."* LSP 3.18 line 73 repeats it verbatim. (The sentence is defective as written — the trailing clause plainly means "batch requests" — but the prohibition is unambiguous.) LSP 3.17's specification.md carries no `batch` string at all; the rule was only written down explicitly when the base protocol was factored out. So the "no batch" rule is real, normative, and recent-ish, not folklore.
32	
33	2. **LSP's compensations for the absent batch are three, and all three are useful precedent.** (i) `$/cancelRequest` — the client withdraws a request whose result is stale; *"A request that got canceled still needs to return from the server and send a response back."* (ii) `partialResultToken` — *"the whole result must be reported using n `$/progress` notifications. Each of the n `$/progress` notification appends items to the result"*, i.e. streaming instead of one big payload. (iii) Lazy resolve, added in 3.17: `workspace/symbol` may return `WorkspaceSymbol` whose `location: Location | { uri: DocumentUri }` omits the range, and *"Clients then need to resolve the range when necessary using the `workspaceSymbol/resolve` request. Servers can only use this new model if clients advertise support for it via the `workspace.symbol.resolveSupport` capability."* This is the "cheap list now, expensive detail on demand" pattern — a strictly better budget lever than truncation, because nothing is dropped.
34	
35	3. **No LSP-successor batching proposal exists that I could find.** Searches across microsoft/language-server-protocol issues/PRs surfaced nothing proposing batch requests. The successor work went the other way: the Base Protocol was extracted (0.9) so DAP/BSP could share it, and it kept the prohibition. Treat "protocols in this family do not batch" as the status quo, with the caveat that absence of a found proposal is weak evidence.
36	
37	4. **MCP also has no batch tool call, and the 2026-07-28 RC does not add one.** The 2025-11-25 tools spec defines exactly one `tools/call` per request, and pagination (`cursor`/`nextCursor`) is defined *only* on list operations — `tools/list` "supports pagination"; `tools/call` results have no cursor field. The 2026-07-28 RC is described as the largest revision since launch but its changes are statelessness (removing the initialize handshake and `Mcp-Session-Id`), an extensions framework, Tasks and Apps, and deprecating Roots/Sampling/Logging. Nothing about batching or paginated tool results. **Consequence: batching for an agent can only live *inside* one tool call.** That is a structural argument for a composite tool, not merely a stylistic one.
38	
39	5. **MCP gives exactly one sanctioned home for a machine-readable envelope: `structuredContent`.** Spec: *"Structured content is returned as a JSON object in the `structuredContent` field of a result"*; *"For backwards compatibility, a tool that returns structured content SHOULD also return the serialized JSON in a TextContent block"*; with an `outputSchema`, *"Servers MUST provide structured results that conform to this schema"* and *"Clients SHOULD validate structured results against this schema."* The spec defines **no** truncation or "there is more" signalling for tool results at all — that is entirely a server-side convention. Michi already produces `structured_content` from `render(OutputFormat::Json)` and already has the `schemars` feature for `outputSchema`, so the slot exists and is unused for this purpose.
40	
41	6. **DataLoader's contract is an ordering contract, and it is the piece worth copying.** README: the batch function *"accepts an Array of keys, and returns a Promise which resolves to an Array of values"*; *"The Array of values must be the same length as the Array of keys. Each index in the Array of values must correspond to the same index in the Array of keys."* Coalescing is per event-loop tick: *"DataLoader will coalesce all individual loads which occur within a single frame of execution."* Caching is deliberately request-scoped: *"DataLoader instances are created when a Request begins, and are not used once the Request ends"*, *"instances should be created per request"*, and *"Avoid multiple requests from different users using the DataLoader instance, which could result in cached data incorrectly appearing in each request."*
42	
43	7. **DataLoader's cache-scope warning maps directly onto Monokl's long-lived `Workspace`.** DataLoader confines its cache to one request precisely because a longer-lived cache serves stale/cross-tenant data. Monokl's `Workspace` is the opposite — long-lived by design (proposal 1, daemon). The correct translation is not "scope the cache to the batch" but "make the batch's *view* immutable": each `query()` executes against one snapshot, so results within a batch are mutually consistent even though the `Workspace` outlives them. DataLoader gets this for free from request lifetime; Monokl must build it. **DataLoader supplies zero prior art for a shared token budget** — it batches and dedupes, it does not ration.
44	
45	8. **rust-analyzer's crate boundary is the sharpest available statement of the plumbing/porcelain split, and it is stricter than proposal 6.** From `docs/book/src/contributing/architecture.md`: `crates/ide` is an **API Boundary**; *"If you want to use IDE parts of rust-analyzer via LSP, custom flatbuffers-based protocol or just as a library in your text editor, this is the right API."* **Architecture Invariant:** *"`ide` crate strives to provide a perfect API. Although at the moment it has only one consumer, the LSP server, LSP does not influence its API design."* And on the presentation crate: **Architecture Invariant:** *"`rust-analyzer` is the only crate that knows about LSP and JSON serialization. If you want to expose a data structure `X` from ide to LSP, don't make it serializable. The interface to Porcelain commands on the other hand are subject to change in order to improve the end user experience."* Wisp is a scripted consumer of Monokl. It therefore wants the plumbing interface, and wants Monokl free to churn the agent-facing porcelain without breaking Wisp.
48	
49	10. **Monokl currently has no such split, and the caps are hardcoded constants in the pipeline.** `pipeline::symbols` hardcodes `per_file_cap = 50`, `total_cap = 500`, and emits a literal string `"[symbol cap 500 reached; pass fewer files or increase limit]"` — neither cap is a parameter. `pipeline::dependents` hardcodes `Cap = 200` and `"[results capped at 200; {tot_dep} dependents, {tot_imp} imports total]"`. `budget::apply_budget` defaults `max_results.unwrap_or(50)` and `max_tokens.unwrap_or(20_000)`, hard-ceilings `max_bytes.min(2_097_152)`, and returns `truncation_marker: Some(format!("[+{omitted} more results omitted; refine with +term or -term]"))`. 51	11. **The agent-tool literature is decisively against large catalogs and silent about single-digit ones.** RAG-MCP (arXiv 2505.03275): tool-selection accuracy 43.13% with retrieval vs **13.62% presenting all tools** vs 18.20% keyword baseline; prompt tokens 1,084 vs 2,133.84; the stress test shows >90% success at ≤30 tools, instability at 31–70, and significant degradation past ~100. "How Many Tools Should an LLM Agent See?" (arXiv 2605.24660): on BFCL's 370 tools, adaptive selection reached "90.3±2.4% coverage at K=7.4", "nearly matching FK=50 (90.8%)" at **7× less depth**; downstream tool-choice accuracy 93.1±0.5% (adaptive) vs 87.1% (fixed K=5), widening to 76.8% vs 60.9% on medium-difficulty queries. MCPGAUGE reports MCP integration degrading effectiveness by roughly 9.5% on average across domains. **None of these ablates 1 vs 3 vs 8 tools.** The measured regime is tens-to-thousands. Anyone citing them to argue "collapse to one tool" is overreading.
52	
53	12. **Anthropic's own tool-design guidance says consolidate, and gives a shape for it.** `writing-tools-for-agents`: *"More tools don't always lead to better outcomes"*; *"Too many tools or overlapping tools can also distract agents"*; and the concrete recommendation to replace `list_users` + `list_events` + `create_event` with a single `schedule_event`. On envelopes: *"implementing some combination of pagination, range selection, filtering, and/or truncation with sensible default parameter values"*; Claude Code restricts tool responses to 25,000 tokens by default; and a `response_format` enum (`"concise"` | `"detailed"`) lets the agent pick, with the concise form costing roughly one-third the tokens. On scale: *"Namespacing (grouping related tools under common prefixes) can help delineate boundaries between lots of tools."*
54	
55	13. **`code-execution-with-MCP` is the strongest argument for a batch API, and it is about intermediate results, not tool count.** *"Every intermediate result must pass through the model"*; a 2-hour meeting transcript routed through two tools *"could mean processing an additional 50,000 tokens"*; the worked example goes *"from 150,000 tokens to 2,000 tokens—a time and cost saving of 98.7%"*. The fix is to *"process data in the execution environment before passing results back to the model"* and express *"complex logic in a single step"*. A Monokl in-process batch is exactly this with the execution environment being Wisp's own process: 10 ops, one result, zero intermediates in context. **This is the load-bearing justification for proposal 2 — stronger than the token-budget argument the proposal actually makes.**
56	
57	14. **Sourcegraph's MCP server is 13 tools, and Sourcegraph itself cut the *default* set to 8 for context reasons.** Full set: `read_file`, `list_files`, `list_repos`, `keyword_search`, `nls_search`, `go_to_definition`, `find_references`, `commit_search`, `diff_search`, `compare_revisions`, `get_contributor_repos`, `deepsearch`, `deepsearch_read`. Docs: *"All tools implement result limits to prevent context window overflow. For large result sets, use pagination cursors (`after`/`before`) or narrow your search with more specific filters"*; `read_file` caps at 128 KB. The March 2026 changelog moved the full suite to `/.api/mcp/all` and left `/.api/mcp` with eight — `read_file`, `list_files`, `keyword_search`, `nls_search`, `list_repos`, `commit_search`, `diff_search`, `deepsearch_read` — because it *"reduces tool-list noise for MCP clients and avoids spending context window budget on lower-frequency tools that most agents do not need by default."* Note precisely which tools got demoted: `go_to_definition` and `find_references`, the code-navigation pair. **The vendor answer is "curate the default, keep the granular surface behind a second endpoint" — not "collapse to one tool".**
58	
59	15. **Serena is the counter-example: 48 tools across 7 categories, with the docs conceding it does not work.** `symbol_tools` (13, incl. `find_symbol`, `find_declaration`, `find_implementations`, `find_referencing_symbols`, `get_symbols_overview`, `get_diagnostics_for_file`, `insert_before_symbol`, `insert_after_symbol`, `replace_symbol_body`, `rename_symbol`, `safe_delete_symbol`), `jetbrains_tools` (13, all optional), `file_tools` (10), `memory_tools` (6), `config_tools` (4), `workflow_tools` (3), `cmd_tools` (1), `query_project_tools` (2). The docs state: *"Note that in most configurations, only a subset of these tools will be enabled simultaneously."* That is a project shipping 48 tools and then telling operators to turn most off — the tool-count problem admitted in the documentation.
60	
61	16. **Serena's overflow behavior is a hard fail, and Wisp must not copy it.** `find_symbol`'s `max_answer_chars`: *"Max characters for the JSON result. If exceeded, no content is returned. -1 means the default value from the config will be used."* The agent gets nothing and must guess a narrower query. Monokl's `truncation_marker` — partial results plus an explicit marker naming the omitted count and the refinement operator — is strictly better and should be defended as a differentiator.
62	
63	17. **Nobody ships a composite "everything about symbol X" tool.** Across Sourcegraph (13), Serena (48), GitNexus (16), Octocode (14), CodeGraph variants (7 to 42), no surveyed server exposes one call returning definition + references + dependents + tests. Serena comes closest and still requires `find_symbol` → `find_referencing_symbols` → `read_file`, three model round-trips with two intermediate payloads in context. Combined with finding 13, **the composite briefing is Wisp's actual differentiation, and Monokl's batch API is its enabler.**
64	
65	18. **Nobody attaches a single top-level budget report across multiple result sections either.** Sourcegraph: per-tool limits and per-tool cursors. Serena: per-tool `max_answer_chars`. MCP: nothing. LSP: nothing. Monokl today: a per-response `truncated`/`truncation_marker`/`total_bytes`/`total_tokens` on `SearchResponse`, a separate `truncation_marker` on `SymbolsResult`, a third on `DependentsResult` — three incompatible shapes, no cross-op notion. A cross-section budget report is **unprecedented in the surveyed prior art**. That is an opportunity and a risk: no one has validated an allocation policy.
66	
67	19. **Michi's `AgentResponse` cannot represent a multi-section response today — this is a hard structural gap, verified in source.** `crates/michi-core/src/response.rs:31` — the struct holds one `type_name: String`, one TOON slot (`items: Vec<Vec<Value>>` + `fields: Vec<String>`), one KV slot (`single_item: Vec<KvItem>`), one `total_count: Option<usize>`, and `enum RenderTarget { Unset, Toon, Kv }` (line 19) selecting between them. `items()` (line 65) sets `target = RenderTarget::Toon`; `kv_items()` (line 81) sets `Kv`. `render()` *"Dispatches on which of `.items()`/`.kv_items()` was called last"* — so calling both loses one. A 10-op batch response is not expressible as one `AgentResponse`.
68	
69	20. **Michi's truncation model is per-string, not per-response.** `michi-truncate::Truncated { content, original_len, was_truncated, signal }` is a string-level result, and `AgentResponse::truncate_cells_at(limit)` (default `DEFAULT_TRUNCATE_CELLS = 200`, line 26) is a per-*cell* clamp on the TOON path only. There is no response-level truncation record anywhere in `michi-core`. The only "there is more" signal on the envelope is `total_count: Option<usize>` — a bare integer with no relation to a budget, no per-section breakdown, and no way to say *why* content was dropped. Monokl's richer truncation information would have to be flattened into a free-text `hint()`.
70	
71	21. **Michi already has the right shape for per-op failure, in the wrong module.** `michi-core::idempotency` defines `PartialSuccess { completed: Vec<String>, failed: Vec<FailedOp>, skipped: Vec<String> }` with `FailedOp { operation, reason, recovery: Option<RecoveryHint> }` and `exit_code() // 0 = no failures, 1 = any failed`. That is exactly the completed/failed/skipped trichotomy a batch response needs. It should be reused for batch outcomes rather than a parallel type being invented — though `Vec<String>` for `completed`/`skipped` is too weak to index results positionally (finding 6).
72	
73	22. **Michi's MCP envelope is already correct and needs no change to carry this.** Per `04-mcp-and-napi.md`, `CallToolResult { content: Vec<ContentBlock>, is_error: bool, structured_content: String }`, with `ContentBlock.audience: Vec<Audience>` matching MCP's array-typed `annotations.audience`, serialization through private `*Wire` structs that add the `"type": "text"` discriminator and nest `audience` under `annotations`, and `structured_content` parsed into embedded JSON rather than double-encoded. `to_call_tool_result()` already emits an assistant block, an optional user block, and `structured_content` from `render(OutputFormat::Json)`. The gap is purely in what `AgentResponse` can *hold*, not in how it serializes.
74	
75	## Verdict on proposed changes
76	
77	**Proposal 2 — batch query `ws.query(&[Op]) -> QueryResponse` with one shared budget and one truncation record: confirm, and strengthen the justification.**
78	
79	The proposal's stated motive (one shared token budget) is the *weakest* of the three real motives. The two stronger ones are: (i) **intermediate results never enter the model's context** — the 150,000→2,000-token argument from `code-execution-with-MCP` (finding 13), which is the whole reason a briefing beats three tool calls; and (ii) **snapshot atomicity** — 10 separate calls against a long-lived `Workspace` can straddle a file edit and produce a briefing whose sections disagree, which is precisely what rust-analyzer's `AnalysisHost`/`Analysis` split exists to prevent (finding 8). Refine the proposal to say so, and to make the snapshot an explicit part of the contract.
80	
81	Concrete shape (question **(a)**):
82	
83	```rust
84	// ---- request ----
85	pub struct QueryRequest<'a> {
86	    pub ops: &'a [Op],
87	    pub budget: Budget,             // ONE budget for the whole batch
88	    pub policy: BudgetPolicy,       // how it is divided
89	    pub deadline: Option<Instant>,  // see rec. 6
90	}
91	
92	pub enum Op {
93	    Symbols    { files: Vec<Utf8PathBuf>, detail: Detail },
94	    Definition { symbol: SymbolId },
95	    Refs       { symbol: SymbolId, detail: Detail },
96	    Dependents { file: Utf8PathBuf },
97	    Imports    { file: Utf8PathBuf },
98	    Search     { query: String, filter: SearchFilter },
99	    Extract    { file: Utf8PathBuf, span: Option<LineSpan> },
100	}
101	
102	/// The budget's degrade-before-drop lever (LSP `workspaceSymbol/resolve`, finding 2).
103	pub enum Detail { Lite, Full }
104	
105	pub enum BudgetPolicy {
106	    /// Caller-declared weights, index-parallel to `ops`.
107	    Weighted(Vec<u16>),
108	    /// Equal share, unused remainder redistributed. Default.
109	    Proportional,
110	    /// Strict priority: earlier ops eat first. Starves the tail — for one-op-matters cases.
111	    Ordered,
112	}
113	
114	// ---- response ----
115	pub struct QueryResponse {
116	    /// INVARIANT: `results.len() == ops.len()`, and `results[i]` answers `ops[i]`.
117	    /// Holds for failed and skipped ops too. (DataLoader ordering contract, finding 6.)
118	    pub results: Vec<OpOutcome>,
119	    /// ONE record for the whole batch — not one per op.
120	    pub budget: BudgetReport,
121	    /// ONE fingerprint: the whole batch ran against a single snapshot.
122	    /// `ws.is_current(&resp.provenance)` is one check for all N results.
123	    pub provenance: Provenance,
124	    /// Batch-level only (e.g. missing tsconfig). Per-op diagnostics live in the outcome.
125	    pub diagnostics: Vec<Diagnostic>,
126	}
127	
128	pub enum OpOutcome {
129	    Ok(OpResult),
130	    Failed  { error: MonoklError },
131	    Skipped { reason: SkipReason },   // BudgetExhausted | Unsupported | Deadline | NotIndexed
132	}
133	
134	pub enum OpResult {
135	    Symbols(SymbolsResult), Definition(DefinitionResult), Refs(RefsResult),
136	    Dependents(DependentsResult), Imports(ImportsResult),
137	    Search(SearchResult), Extract(Vec<CodeBlock>),
138	}
139	
140	pub struct BudgetReport {
141	    pub limits: Budget,
142	    pub tokens_used: usize,
143	    pub bytes_used: usize,
144	    /// Index-parallel to `ops`.
145	    pub per_op: Vec<OpBudget>,
146	    pub truncated: bool,       // any op truncated or skipped
147	}
148	
149	pub struct OpBudget {
150	    pub tokens: usize,
151	    pub bytes: usize,
152	    pub items_returned: usize,
153	    pub items_total: usize,     // pre-truncation
154	    pub detail_degraded: bool,  // Full was requested, Lite was served
155	}
156	```
157	
158	Four deliberate choices. **First, no `truncation_marker: Option<String>` anywhere.** Monokl today emits three different pre-rendered English strings from the analysis layer (finding 10); the batch response should carry `items_returned`/`items_total` and let the porcelain render one marker. **Second, per-op failure never fails the batch** — `OpOutcome` is Result-shaped per index, mirroring `PartialSuccess`'s completed/failed/skipped (finding 21) while keeping positional indexing that `Vec<String>` loses. **Third, one `Provenance` for the batch**, which is only sound because of the snapshot; it also makes proposal 4's `ws.is_current()` a single call per briefing instead of N. **Fourth, `Detail` on the ops that support it**, so the budget can degrade before it drops (finding 2) — Monokl already has `symbols --lite`, so this is formalizing an existing capability, not new work.
159	
160	Implementation note: `apply_budget` currently tokenizes every candidate block with tiktoken before deciding. Across a 10-op batch that is the dominant cost. Prefilter by `code.len()` bytes (already free) and only tokenize candidates that survive the byte filter — the existing loop already tracks both, so this is a reordering, not a redesign.
161	
162	**Proposal 6 — split raw-analysis API from agent-facing API: confirm, and go further than proposed.**
163	
164	rust-analyzer and git both draw this line, and rust-analyzer draws it harder than proposal 6 does: not two method families on one type, but **two crates**, with the presentation types *not shared* (finding 8). Monokl violates this today — `types.rs` derives `Serialize` on the core result types, and `output.rs` puts `serde_json` and `println!` in the library (finding 10).
165	
166	Answer to question **(d)**:
167	
168	- **`monokl-core` (plumbing).** `Workspace`, `Analysis` snapshots, `Arc<FileAnalysis>`, the import graph and symbol index, `LanguageAnalyzer`, and *fully ranked, deduped, uncapped* results. No `tiktoken`, no serde derives on result types, no caps, no rendered strings, no `println!`. Stable interface, because Wisp is a scripted consumer (finding 9). This is where `ws.analysis(path) -> Arc<FileAnalysis>` lives.
169	- **`monokl-agent` (porcelain).** `Budget`, `BudgetPolicy`, `apply_budget`, tiktoken, the `Detail` degrade path, truncation marker rendering, Michi integration, the CLI, and the MCP server if there is one. Owns the wire types and converts by hand from `monokl-core`'s POD types. Free to churn.
170	
171	**Do Monokl's 50/500 symbol caps belong in the library? No — but the *ranking* does.** The distinction matters and the proposal blurs it. `pipeline::symbols`'s `per_file_cap = 50` / `total_cap = 500` are pure policy on an unordered set: nothing distinguishes the 50 symbols kept from the ones dropped, so the cap destroys information for no analytical reason. Delete them from the library outright. `budget::apply_budget`'s `max_results = 50` is different — it truncates a **BM25-ranked** list, so "the first 50" is a meaningful answer. Keep the ranking in `monokl-core` (`search()` returns the full ranked `Vec<RankedBlock>`); move the cutting to `monokl-agent`, with no defaults baked into the function. `Budget::agent_default()` in the porcelain crate can hold today's 50 / 20,000 / 2 MiB. Per Anthropic's guidance the cap should be a parameter with a sensible default, and `response_format: concise | detailed` should be the agent-facing knob over it (finding 12).
172	
173	Same treatment for `dependents`'s `Cap = 200`: `monokl-core` returns all dependents; `monokl-agent` cuts and reports.
174	
175	**Proposal 9 — shared `orin-contracts` crate: refine.**
176	
177	The permissive-license motive is sound and independent — Michi is AGPL, Monokl is AGPL, and a shared vocabulary crate that Wisp and third-party harness plugins can depend on needs to be permissive. But finding 8 cuts against putting *result types* in it: rust-analyzer's invariant is explicitly *"don't make it serializable. Instead, create a serializable counterpart in [the presentation crate] and manually convert between the two."* A shared serde-derived contracts crate pulls wire concerns back into the analysis layer, which is the thing the split exists to prevent.
178	
179	Refinement: `orin-contracts` holds **vocabulary only** — `CapabilityPrecision`, `ContentHash`, `Diagnostic`/`DiagnosticKind`, `Provenance`, the `Truncation`/`BudgetReport` shape, and the pinned artifact JSON schemas. Value types, no behavior, serde-derived because they *are* the wire format. Monokl's rich result types (`SymbolsResult`, `RankedBlock`, `FileAnalysis`) stay in `monokl-core`, unshared and *not* `Serialize`; their wire counterparts are built in `monokl-agent`. The test: if a type is something Wisp and Monokl must *agree on the meaning of*, it goes in contracts; if it is something Monokl *computes*, it does not.
180	
181	## Answers to the direct questions
182	
183	**(b) One `wisp_brief` MCP tool, or several? — Three, not one, and not eight.**
184	
185	The evidence is real but narrower than it looks. Findings 11–12 establish that *large catalogs* hurt (13.62% at full catalog vs 43.13% with retrieval; degradation past ~30 tools; ~9.5% average MCP degradation) and that consolidation is the right instinct. **No study ablates 1 vs 3.** So the literature rules out eight-plus and says nothing about the difference between one and three; that call is judgment, made on three concrete grounds:
186	
187	1. **Sourcegraph, the closest analogue with real usage data, chose curation over collapse** (finding 14): eight tools on the default endpoint, thirteen behind `/.api/mcp/all`. They demoted `go_to_definition` and `find_references` — the exact operations Wisp would fold into a briefing — but kept them reachable.
188	2. **A single tool with a `mode` enum re-creates the tool-selection problem inside the input schema**, where it is worse: the agent still chooses, but from an under-described enum variant instead of a tool with its own description, `outputSchema`, and annotations.
189	3. **The three surfaces have genuinely different cost and cardinality.** A briefing is expensive and called once per stage; a freshness check is nearly free and called repeatedly; artifact read/write is a different trust class (canonical, mutating).
190	
191	Recommended surface:
192	
193	- **`wisp_brief`** — the composite. Takes a stage and an artifact reference, internally issues one Monokl `query(&[Op])` batch, and returns the cited briefing. Per finding 17 this is the "everything about X" call **nobody ships**, and per finding 13 its value is that the ten intermediate results never enter the model's context. Give it `response_format: concise | detailed` (finding 12) and `detail: lite | full` mapping onto `Op::Detail`.
194	- **`wisp_artifacts`** — list, read, validate, and write `spec@1`/`plan@1`/etc. Separate because it mutates and because it is the canonical-provenance surface.
195	- **`wisp_check`** — freshness/provenance verification against a `Provenance` the agent already holds. Cheap, high-frequency, and separating it means an agent can re-verify without re-paying for a briefing.
196	
197	Namespace them all `wisp_*` per finding 12. And **Monokl should not ship a six-tool MCP server mirroring its six subcommands** — that is the Serena failure mode (finding 15). If Monokl exposes MCP at all, it should be one or two tools over the batch API.
198	
199	**(c) What Michi needs to be the envelope for both Monokl batch results and Wisp briefings.**
200	
201	Five additions. Michi's MCP serialization is already correct (finding 22); the gap is entirely in what `AgentResponse` can hold.
202	
203	1. **Multi-section support — the blocking gap** (finding 19). Today `RenderTarget` is `Unset | Toon | Kv` and `render()` dispatches on whichever of `items()`/`kv_items()` ran last, so a 10-section response silently loses nine. Add a repeatable `section()`:
204	
205	   ```rust
206	   pub struct Section {
207	       pub name: String,
208	       pub body: SectionBody,          // Toon { fields, rows } | Kv(Vec<KvItem>) | Text(String)
209	       pub returned_count: usize,
210	       pub total_count: Option<usize>, // Some(n) with n > returned_count ⇒ "there is more"
211	       pub truncated: bool,
212	   }
213	   impl AgentResponse { pub fn section(self, s: Section) -> Self; }
214	   ```
215	
216	   Keep `items()`/`kv_items()` as the one-section sugar so nothing breaks — they become `section(Section::toon(...))` with the existing `type_name`.
217	
218	2. **A response-level `BudgetReport` slot** (finding 20). Today the only envelope-level "there is more" signal is a bare `total_count: Option<usize>`, and Monokl's truncation information can only reach the agent as free-text `hint()`. Add `pub fn budget(self, b: BudgetReport) -> Self`, rendered once as a `budget:` KV block plus per-section `returned/total`. This is the **single top-level budget report across sections** that finding 18 shows nobody has — it is Michi's job precisely because Michi is the shared layer both Monokl and Wisp render through.
219	
220	3. **A `Provenance` slot** — one per response, not one per row: fingerprint, precision, freshness class, version. Rendered as a KV block. Wisp's provenance-class rule and Monokl's `WorkspaceFingerprint` both land here, and per finding 7 a batch has exactly one because it has exactly one snapshot.
221	
222	4. **Per-op outcome rendering, reusing `PartialSuccess`** (finding 21) rather than a new type — but widen `completed`/`skipped` from `Vec<String>` to something index-bearing so `results[i] ↔ ops[i]` survives into the rendered output.
223	
224	5. **Populate `structuredContent` with the envelope, and ship an `outputSchema`** (finding 5). `to_call_tool_result()` already emits `structured_content` from `render(OutputFormat::Json)`; extend that JSON to carry `sections[]`, `budget`, and `provenance`, and use the existing `schemars` feature to publish the `outputSchema` so clients can validate — the spec makes conformance a MUST once a schema is declared.
225	
226	**Explicit non-requirement:** do not add pagination cursors. MCP defines them only for list operations (finding 4), so a cursor on a `tools/call` result is a private convention the client will not honor. Truncation + counts + a refinement hint is the right signal, and it must never be Serena's "no content is returned" (finding 16).
227	
228	## Recommendations not on the list
229	
230	1. **Define the batch as executing against one immutable snapshot, and say so in the type.** `Workspace::query` should internally take an `Analysis`-style snapshot (rust-analyzer's `AnalysisHost`/`Analysis`, finding 8) so all N results are mutually consistent and share one `Provenance`. Without this, a 10-op batch on a long-lived daemon `Workspace` can straddle an edit and produce a self-contradictory briefing — a correctness bug that N separate calls at least make visible. This is a stronger argument for proposal 2 than the token budget, and it is not in the proposal.
231	
232	2. **Dedupe identical ops within a batch.** DataLoader's per-request cache (finding 6) exists for exactly this. A briefing that asks for `Symbols{a.ts}` and later `Symbols{a.ts}` should compute once and return the same result at both indices. Cheap, and it preserves the index-parallel contract.
233	
234	3. **Degrade detail before dropping results.** LSP 3.17's `workspaceSymbol/resolve` returns symbols without ranges and resolves lazily (finding 2). Monokl's existing `symbols --lite` is the same idea; promote it to a per-op `Detail` and let `apply_budget` step `Full → Lite` before it truncates. For a briefing, twenty lite symbols beat five full ones, and today's `apply_budget` has no such lever.
235	
236	4. **Give `wisp_brief` a `response_format: concise | detailed` parameter.** Anthropic's guidance, with concise measured at roughly one-third the tokens (finding 12). Cheaper than guessing one budget for all callers.
237	
238	5. **Add a deadline to `query()` and mark unfinished ops `Skipped { Deadline }`.** Batching introduces head-of-line blocking that N separate calls do not have — one pathological op stalls the briefing. LSP's `$/cancelRequest` exists for this class of problem (finding 2), and Monokl needs the in-process equivalent. Without it the batch's failure mode is strictly worse than the status quo.
239	
240	6. **Write down the "never fail-closed on overflow" rule as a project principle.** Serena returns nothing when `max_answer_chars` is exceeded (finding 16). Monokl already does better. Make it explicit so neither Wisp nor a future Monokl op regresses to it.
241	
242	7. **Consider streaming for the daemon case.** LSP's `partialResultToken` appends items via `$/progress` notifications (finding 2). Not needed for v1 CLI briefings, but if the daemon (proposal 1) ever serves an interactive client, the batch response is a large one-shot payload and this is the established alternative.
243	
244	## Contradictions and open questions
245	
246	- **The tool-count evidence does not reach the question actually being asked.** RAG-MCP, the chance-corrected paper, and MCPGAUGE all operate at 30–3,251 tools. Recommendation (b) — three tools rather than one — rests on Sourcegraph's product decision and on schema-design reasoning, not on measured ablation. If Wisp's Prism paired-evaluation harness (proposal 16) can afford it, a 1-vs-3 tool arm is a cheap and genuinely novel experiment.
247	- **Sourcegraph's behavior cuts both ways.** They pruned the default set (supports consolidation) *and* kept the full granular surface at a second endpoint (cuts against collapsing). The honest reading is "curate the default, keep the primitives reachable" — which for Wisp might mean `wisp_brief` by default with Monokl's finer ops reachable through a second endpoint or a `detail` escape hatch, not that the finer ops should not exist.
248	- **No prior art exists for allocating one token budget across N heterogeneous result sections** (finding 18). DataLoader batches without rationing; MCP and LSP have no cross-call budget; Sourcegraph and Serena are strictly per-tool. `BudgetPolicy` is therefore a guess. Ship `Proportional` as the default, make the policy a parameter, and measure on the proposal-10 benchmark rather than reasoning about it further.
249	- **Snapshot cost is unmeasured.** Recommendation 1 assumes a cheap immutable snapshot. rust-analyzer gets this from salsa; Monokl refolds a `WorkspaceIndex` in memory per invocation and shares `Arc<FileAnalysis>` from a DashMap. Whether "snapshot" means an `Arc` clone of the index (cheap) or a rebuild (not cheap) depends on details of `WorkspaceIndex::build` I did not read. Worth confirming before the contract commits to it.
250	- **The exact MCPGAUGE degradation figure (~9.5%) was read from a search summary, not the paper.** Directionally corroborated by RAG-MCP's 13.62%-at-full-catalog, but do not quote the number without checking arXiv 2508.12566 directly.
251	- **Serena's `max_answer_chars` semantics come from a third-party schema mirror (glama.ai), not Serena's own docs.** The official tools page did not state overflow behavior. The quoted text reads like generated tool documentation and is probably accurate, but finding 16 is one confirmation short.
252	- **Whether `Op` should be an enum at all.** An enum forces every op into one dispatch and makes `OpResult` a parallel enum the caller must match twice. A trait-object or typed-builder alternative (each op knows its own result type) would be more Rust-idiomatic but breaks the homogeneous `&[Op]` slice and the index-parallel `Vec<OpOutcome>` that finding 6 argues for. I recommend the enum — the ordering contract is worth more than the type-level precision — but this is a real trade-off, not a settled one.
253
