# 05 — Batch query APIs, agent-facing tool surfaces, result envelopes

Scope: proposals 2 (batch query), 6 (raw-vs-budgeted split), 9 (shared contracts crate). Questions answered: (a) `Op` enum + response shape, (b) one `wisp_brief` tool vs several, (c) what Michi must add, (d) Monokl plumbing/porcelain split.

## Sources read

- `/Users/gabe/Projects/monokl/docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md` §10 `budget.rs`, §20 `pipeline.rs`, §21 `cli.rs`/`output.rs`, §4 `types.rs` — confirmed
- `/Users/gabe/Projects/michi/README.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/spec/03-rust-api.md`, `docs/spec/04-mcp-and-napi.md` — confirmed
- `/Users/gabe/Projects/michi/crates/michi-core/src/response.rs` (source, lines 1–70 + public-fn index) — confirmed
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/language-server-protocol/gh-pages/_specifications/lsp/3.18/specification.md line 73 — confirmed
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/language-server-protocol/gh-pages/_specifications/base/0.9/specification.md line 122 — confirmed
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/microsoft/language-server-protocol/gh-pages/_specifications/lsp/3.17/workspace/symbol.md (`workspaceSymbol/resolve`, `resolveSupport`) — confirmed
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rust-lang/rust-analyzer/master/docs/book/src/contributing/architecture.md §`crates/ide`, §`crates/rust-analyzer` — confirmed
- https://git-scm.com/docs/git (plumbing/porcelain stability guarantee) — confirmed
- https://github.com/graphql/dataloader README (batch function contract, per-request lifetime) — confirmed
- https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools (`structuredContent`, `outputSchema`, `isError`, pagination scope) — confirmed
- https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents — confirmed
- https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/code-execution-with-mcp — confirmed
- https://sourcegraph-docs.mintlify.app/api/mcp (Sourcegraph MCP tool inventory) — confirmed (mirror of a 403-gated canonical page)
- https://sourcegraph.com/changelog/mcp-curated-default-tools + `/changelog/mcp-all` (default tool set reduced) — likely (read via search summary; canonical page 403s)
- https://oraios.github.io/serena/01-about/035_tools.html (48 tools, 7 categories) — confirmed
- https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/@oraios/serena/tools/find_symbol (`max_answer_chars` semantics) — likely (third-party schema mirror)
- https://arxiv.org/html/2505.03275v1 RAG-MCP — confirmed
- https://arxiv.org/html/2605.24660v1 "How Many Tools Should an LLM Agent See? A Chance-Corrected Answer" — confirmed
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12566 MCPGAUGE ("Help or Hurdle?") — likely (abstract page only; the 9.5% figure comes from a search-result summary of the full text, not read directly)
- https://rywalker.com/research/code-intelligence-tools (comparative tool-count survey incl. GitNexus 16, Octocode 14) — likely
- https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28-release-candidate/ — likely (read via search summary)

## Findings

1. **LSP forbids JSON-RPC batching outright, in normative language.** Base Protocol 0.9 §"Base Protocol", line 122: *"The base protocol uses request, response, and notification objects as specified in the JSON-RPC protocol. It currently does not support JSON-RPC batch messages; protocol clients and servers must not send JSON-RPC requests."* LSP 3.18 line 73 repeats it verbatim. (The sentence is defective as written — the trailing clause plainly means "batch requests" — but the prohibition is unambiguous.) LSP 3.17's specification.md carries no `batch` string at all; the rule was only written down explicitly when the base protocol was factored out. So the "no batch" rule is real, normative, and recent-ish, not folklore.

2. **LSP's compensations for the absent batch are three, and all three are useful precedent.** (i) `$/cancelRequest` — the client withdraws a request whose result is stale; *"A request that got canceled still needs to return from the server and send a response back."* (ii) `partialResultToken` — *"the whole result must be reported using n `$/progress` notifications. Each of the n `$/progress` notification appends items to the result"*, i.e. streaming instead of one big payload. (iii) Lazy resolve, added in 3.17: `workspace/symbol` may return `WorkspaceSymbol` whose `location: Location | { uri: DocumentUri }` omits the range, and *"Clients then need to resolve the range when necessary using the `workspaceSymbol/resolve` request. Servers can only use this new model if clients advertise support for it via the `workspace.symbol.resolveSupport` capability."* This is the "cheap list now, expensive detail on demand" pattern — a strictly better budget lever than truncation, because nothing is dropped.

3. **No LSP-successor batching proposal exists that I could find.** Searches across microsoft/language-server-protocol issues/PRs surfaced nothing proposing batch requests. The successor work went the other way: the Base Protocol was extracted (0.9) so DAP/BSP could share it, and it kept the prohibition. Treat "protocols in this family do not batch" as the status quo, with the caveat that absence of a found proposal is weak evidence.

4. **MCP also has no batch tool call, and the 2026-07-28 RC does not add one.** The 2025-11-25 tools spec defines exactly one `tools/call` per request, and pagination (`cursor`/`nextCursor`) is defined *only* on list operations — `tools/list` "supports pagination"; `tools/call` results have no cursor field. The 2026-07-28 RC is described as the largest revision since launch but its changes are statelessness (removing the initialize handshake and `Mcp-Session-Id`), an extensions framework, Tasks and Apps, and deprecating Roots/Sampling/Logging. Nothing about batching or paginated tool results. **Consequence: batching for an agent can only live *inside* one tool call.** That is a structural argument for a composite tool, not merely a stylistic one.

5. **MCP gives exactly one sanctioned home for a machine-readable envelope: `structuredContent`.** Spec: *"Structured content is returned as a JSON object in the `structuredContent` field of a result"*; *"For backwards compatibility, a tool that returns structured content SHOULD also return the serialized JSON in a TextContent block"*; with an `outputSchema`, *"Servers MUST provide structured results that conform to this schema"* and *"Clients SHOULD validate structured results against this schema."* The spec defines **no** truncation or "there is more" signalling for tool results at all — that is entirely a server-side convention. Michi already produces `structured_content` from `render(OutputFormat::Json)` and already has the `schemars` feature for `outputSchema`, so the slot exists and is unused for this purpose.

6. **DataLoader's contract is an ordering contract, and it is the piece worth copying.** README: the batch function *"accepts an Array of keys, and returns a Promise which resolves to an Array of values"*; *"The Array of values must be the same length as the Array of keys. Each index in the Array of values must correspond to the same index in the Array of keys."* Coalescing is per event-loop tick: *"DataLoader will coalesce all individual loads which occur within a single frame of execution."* Caching is deliberately request-scoped: *"DataLoader instances are created when a Request begins, and are not used once the Request ends"*, *"instances should be created per request"*, and *"Avoid multiple requests from different users using the DataLoader instance, which could result in cached data incorrectly appearing in each request."*

7. **DataLoader's cache-scope warning maps directly onto Monokl's long-lived `Workspace`.** DataLoader confines its cache to one request precisely because a longer-lived cache serves stale/cross-tenant data. Monokl's `Workspace` is the opposite — long-lived by design (proposal 1, daemon). The correct translation is not "scope the cache to the batch" but "make the batch's *view* immutable": each `query()` executes against one snapshot, so results within a batch are mutually consistent even though the `Workspace` outlives them. DataLoader gets this for free from request lifetime; Monokl must build it. **DataLoader supplies zero prior art for a shared token budget** — it batches and dedupes, it does not ration.

8. **rust-analyzer's crate boundary is the sharpest available statement of the plumbing/porcelain split, and it is stricter than proposal 6.** From `docs/book/src/contributing/architecture.md`: `crates/ide` is an **API Boundary**; *"If you want to use IDE parts of rust-analyzer via LSP, custom flatbuffers-based protocol or just as a library in your text editor, this is the right API."* **Architecture Invariant:** *"`ide` crate strives to provide a perfect API. Although at the moment it has only one consumer, the LSP server, LSP does not influence its API design."* And on the presentation crate: **Architecture Invariant:** *"`rust-analyzer` is the only crate that knows about LSP and JSON serialization. If you want to expose a data structure `X` from ide to LSP, don't make it serializable. Instead, create a serializable counterpart in `rust-analyzer` crate and manually convert between the two."* Also relevant to batching: *"`ide` is also the first crate which has the notion of change over time. `AnalysisHost` is a state to which you can transactionally `apply_change`. `Analysis` is an immutable snapshot of the state."*

9. **Git states the stability rationale for the same split.** `git(1)`: *"We divide Git into high level ("porcelain") commands and low level ("plumbing") commands."* … *"The interface (input, output, set of options and the semantics) to these low-level commands are meant to be a lot more stable than Porcelain level commands, because these commands are primarily for scripted use. The interface to Porcelain commands on the other hand are subject to change in order to improve the end user experience."* Wisp is a scripted consumer of Monokl. It therefore wants the plumbing interface, and wants Monokl free to churn the agent-facing porcelain without breaking Wisp.

10. **Monokl currently has no such split, and the caps are hardcoded constants in the pipeline.** `pipeline::symbols` hardcodes `per_file_cap = 50`, `total_cap = 500`, and emits a literal string `"[symbol cap 500 reached; pass fewer files or increase limit]"` — neither cap is a parameter. `pipeline::dependents` hardcodes `Cap = 200` and `"[results capped at 200; {tot_dep} dependents, {tot_imp} imports total]"`. `budget::apply_budget` defaults `max_results.unwrap_or(50)` and `max_tokens.unwrap_or(20_000)`, hard-ceilings `max_bytes.min(2_097_152)`, and returns `truncation_marker: Some(format!("[+{omitted} more results omitted; refine with +term or -term]"))`. Every one of these is presentation policy expressed as a library constant, and every one emits a pre-rendered English string from the analysis layer. `output.rs` further couples the library to `serde_json` and `println!`, and `types.rs` derives `Serialize` on the core result types — the exact thing rust-analyzer's invariant forbids.

11. **The agent-tool literature is decisively against large catalogs and silent about single-digit ones.** RAG-MCP (arXiv 2505.03275): tool-selection accuracy 43.13% with retrieval vs **13.62% presenting all tools** vs 18.20% keyword baseline; prompt tokens 1,084 vs 2,133.84; the stress test shows >90% success at ≤30 tools, instability at 31–70, and significant degradation past ~100. "How Many Tools Should an LLM Agent See?" (arXiv 2605.24660): on BFCL's 370 tools, adaptive selection reached "90.3±2.4% coverage at K=7.4", "nearly matching FK=50 (90.8%)" at **7× less depth**; downstream tool-choice accuracy 93.1±0.5% (adaptive) vs 87.1% (fixed K=5), widening to 76.8% vs 60.9% on medium-difficulty queries. MCPGAUGE reports MCP integration degrading effectiveness by roughly 9.5% on average across domains. **None of these ablates 1 vs 3 vs 8 tools.** The measured regime is tens-to-thousands. Anyone citing them to argue "collapse to one tool" is overreading.

12. **Anthropic's own tool-design guidance says consolidate, and gives a shape for it.** `writing-tools-for-agents`: *"More tools don't always lead to better outcomes"*; *"Too many tools or overlapping tools can also distract agents"*; and the concrete recommendation to replace `list_users` + `list_events` + `create_event` with a single `schedule_event`. On envelopes: *"implementing some combination of pagination, range selection, filtering, and/or truncation with sensible default parameter values"*; Claude Code restricts tool responses to 25,000 tokens by default; and a `response_format` enum (`"concise"` | `"detailed"`) lets the agent pick, with the concise form costing roughly one-third the tokens. On scale: *"Namespacing (grouping related tools under common prefixes) can help delineate boundaries between lots of tools."*

13. **`code-execution-with-MCP` is the strongest argument for a batch API, and it is about intermediate results, not tool count.** *"Every intermediate result must pass through the model"*; a 2-hour meeting transcript routed through two tools *"could mean processing an additional 50,000 tokens"*; the worked example goes *"from 150,000 tokens to 2,000 tokens—a time and cost saving of 98.7%"*. The fix is to *"process data in the execution environment before passing results back to the model"* and express *"complex logic in a single step"*. A Monokl in-process batch is exactly this with the execution environment being Wisp's own process: 10 ops, one result, zero intermediates in context. **This is the load-bearing justification for proposal 2 — stronger than the token-budget argument the proposal actually makes.**

14. **Sourcegraph's MCP server is 13 tools, and Sourcegraph itself cut the *default* set to 8 for context reasons.** Full set: `read_file`, `list_files`, `list_repos`, `keyword_search`, `nls_search`, `go_to_definition`, `find_references`, `commit_search`, `diff_search`, `compare_revisions`, `get_contributor_repos`, `deepsearch`, `deepsearch_read`. Docs: *"All tools implement result limits to prevent context window overflow. For large result sets, use pagination cursors (`after`/`before`) or narrow your search with more specific filters"*; `read_file` caps at 128 KB. The March 2026 changelog moved the full suite to `/.api/mcp/all` and left `/.api/mcp` with eight — `read_file`, `list_files`, `keyword_search`, `nls_search`, `list_repos`, `commit_search`, `diff_search`, `deepsearch_read` — because it *"reduces tool-list noise for MCP clients and avoids spending context window budget on lower-frequency tools that most agents do not need by default."* Note precisely which tools got demoted: `go_to_definition` and `find_references`, the code-navigation pair. **The vendor answer is "curate the default, keep the granular surface behind a second endpoint" — not "collapse to one tool".**

15. **Serena is the counter-example: 48 tools across 7 categories, with the docs conceding it does not work.** `symbol_tools` (13, incl. `find_symbol`, `find_declaration`, `find_implementations`, `find_referencing_symbols`, `get_symbols_overview`, `get_diagnostics_for_file`, `insert_before_symbol`, `insert_after_symbol`, `replace_symbol_body`, `rename_symbol`, `safe_delete_symbol`), `jetbrains_tools` (13, all optional), `file_tools` (10), `memory_tools` (6), `config_tools` (4), `workflow_tools` (3), `cmd_tools` (1), `query_project_tools` (2). The docs state: *"Note that in most configurations, only a subset of these tools will be enabled simultaneously."* That is a project shipping 48 tools and then telling operators to turn most off — the tool-count problem admitted in the documentation.

16. **Serena's overflow behavior is a hard fail, and Wisp must not copy it.** `find_symbol`'s `max_answer_chars`: *"Max characters for the JSON result. If exceeded, no content is returned. -1 means the default value from the config will be used."* The agent gets nothing and must guess a narrower query. Monokl's `truncation_marker` — partial results plus an explicit marker naming the omitted count and the refinement operator — is strictly better and should be defended as a differentiator.

17. **Nobody ships a composite "everything about symbol X" tool.** Across Sourcegraph (13), Serena (48), GitNexus (16), Octocode (14), CodeGraph variants (7 to 42), no surveyed server exposes one call returning definition + references + dependents + tests. Serena comes closest and still requires `find_symbol` → `find_referencing_symbols` → `read_file`, three model round-trips with two intermediate payloads in context. Combined with finding 13, **the composite briefing is Wisp's actual differentiation, and Monokl's batch API is its enabler.**

18. **Nobody attaches a single top-level budget report across multiple result sections either.** Sourcegraph: per-tool limits and per-tool cursors. Serena: per-tool `max_answer_chars`. MCP: nothing. LSP: nothing. Monokl today: a per-response `truncated`/`truncation_marker`/`total_bytes`/`total_tokens` on `SearchResponse`, a separate `truncation_marker` on `SymbolsResult`, a third on `DependentsResult` — three incompatible shapes, no cross-op notion. A cross-section budget report is **unprecedented in the surveyed prior art**. That is an opportunity and a risk: no one has validated an allocation policy.

19. **Michi's `AgentResponse` cannot represent a multi-section response today — this is a hard structural gap, verified in source.** `crates/michi-core/src/response.rs:31` — the struct holds one `type_name: String`, one TOON slot (`items: Vec<Vec<Value>>` + `fields: Vec<String>`), one KV slot (`single_item: Vec<KvItem>`), one `total_count: Option<usize>`, and `enum RenderTarget { Unset, Toon, Kv }` (line 19) selecting between them. `items()` (line 65) sets `target = RenderTarget::Toon`; `kv_items()` (line 81) sets `Kv`. `render()` *"Dispatches on which of `.items()`/`.kv_items()` was called last"* — so calling both loses one. A 10-op batch response is not expressible as one `AgentResponse`.

20. **Michi's truncation model is per-string, not per-response.** `michi-truncate::Truncated { content, original_len, was_truncated, signal }` is a string-level result, and `AgentResponse::truncate_cells_at(limit)` (default `DEFAULT_TRUNCATE_CELLS = 200`, line 26) is a per-*cell* clamp on the TOON path only. There is no response-level truncation record anywhere in `michi-core`. The only "there is more" signal on the envelope is `total_count: Option<usize>` — a bare integer with no relation to a budget, no per-section breakdown, and no way to say *why* content was dropped. Monokl's richer truncation information would have to be flattened into a free-text `hint()`.

21. **Michi already has the right shape for per-op failure, in the wrong module.** `michi-core::idempotency` defines `PartialSuccess { completed: Vec<String>, failed: Vec<FailedOp>, skipped: Vec<String> }` with `FailedOp { operation, reason, recovery: Option<RecoveryHint> }` and `exit_code() // 0 = no failures, 1 = any failed`. That is exactly the completed/failed/skipped trichotomy a batch response needs. It should be reused for batch outcomes rather than a parallel type being invented — though `Vec<String>` for `completed`/`skipped` is too weak to index results positionally (finding 6).

22. **Michi's MCP envelope is already correct and needs no change to carry this.** Per `04-mcp-and-napi.md`, `CallToolResult { content: Vec<ContentBlock>, is_error: bool, structured_content: String }`, with `ContentBlock.audience: Vec<Audience>` matching MCP's array-typed `annotations.audience`, serialization through private `*Wire` structs that add the `"type": "text"` discriminator and nest `audience` under `annotations`, and `structured_content` parsed into embedded JSON rather than double-encoded. `to_call_tool_result()` already emits an assistant block, an optional user block, and `structured_content` from `render(OutputFormat::Json)`. The gap is purely in what `AgentResponse` can *hold*, not in how it serializes.

## Verdict on proposed changes

**Proposal 2 — batch query `ws.query(&[Op]) -> QueryResponse` with one shared budget and one truncation record: confirm, and strengthen the justification.**

The proposal's stated motive (one shared token budget) is the *weakest* of the three real motives. The two stronger ones are: (i) **intermediate results never enter the model's context** — the 150,000→2,000-token argument from `code-execution-with-MCP` (finding 13), which is the whole reason a briefing beats three tool calls; and (ii) **snapshot atomicity** — 10 separate calls against a long-lived `Workspace` can straddle a file edit and produce a briefing whose sections disagree, which is precisely what rust-analyzer's `AnalysisHost`/`Analysis` split exists to prevent (finding 8). Refine the proposal to say so, and to make the snapshot an explicit part of the contract.

Concrete shape (question **(a)**):

```rust
// ---- request ----
pub struct QueryRequest<'a> {
    pub ops: &'a [Op],
    pub budget: Budget,             // ONE budget for the whole batch
    pub policy: BudgetPolicy,       // how it is divided
    pub deadline: Option<Instant>,  // see rec. 6
}

pub enum Op {
    Symbols    { files: Vec<Utf8PathBuf>, detail: Detail },
    Definition { symbol: SymbolId },
    Refs       { symbol: SymbolId, detail: Detail },
    Dependents { file: Utf8PathBuf },
    Imports    { file: Utf8PathBuf },
    Search     { query: String, filter: SearchFilter },
    Extract    { file: Utf8PathBuf, span: Option<LineSpan> },
}

/// The budget's degrade-before-drop lever (LSP `workspaceSymbol/resolve`, finding 2).
pub enum Detail { Lite, Full }

pub enum BudgetPolicy {
    /// Caller-declared weights, index-parallel to `ops`.
    Weighted(Vec<u16>),
    /// Equal share, unused remainder redistributed. Default.
    Proportional,
    /// Strict priority: earlier ops eat first. Starves the tail — for one-op-matters cases.
    Ordered,
}

// ---- response ----
pub struct QueryResponse {
    /// INVARIANT: `results.len() == ops.len()`, and `results[i]` answers `ops[i]`.
    /// Holds for failed and skipped ops too. (DataLoader ordering contract, finding 6.)
    pub results: Vec<OpOutcome>,
    /// ONE record for the whole batch — not one per op.
    pub budget: BudgetReport,
    /// ONE fingerprint: the whole batch ran against a single snapshot.
    /// `ws.is_current(&resp.provenance)` is one check for all N results.
    pub provenance: Provenance,
    /// Batch-level only (e.g. missing tsconfig). Per-op diagnostics live in the outcome.
    pub diagnostics: Vec<Diagnostic>,
}

pub enum OpOutcome {
    Ok(OpResult),
    Failed  { error: MonoklError },
    Skipped { reason: SkipReason },   // BudgetExhausted | Unsupported | Deadline | NotIndexed
}

pub enum OpResult {
    Symbols(SymbolsResult), Definition(DefinitionResult), Refs(RefsResult),
    Dependents(DependentsResult), Imports(ImportsResult),
    Search(SearchResult), Extract(Vec<CodeBlock>),
}

pub struct BudgetReport {
    pub limits: Budget,
    pub tokens_used: usize,
    pub bytes_used: usize,
    /// Index-parallel to `ops`.
    pub per_op: Vec<OpBudget>,
    pub truncated: bool,       // any op truncated or skipped
}

pub struct OpBudget {
    pub tokens: usize,
    pub bytes: usize,
    pub items_returned: usize,
    pub items_total: usize,     // pre-truncation
    pub detail_degraded: bool,  // Full was requested, Lite was served
}
```

Four deliberate choices. **First, no `truncation_marker: Option<String>` anywhere.** Monokl today emits three different pre-rendered English strings from the analysis layer (finding 10); the batch response should carry `items_returned`/`items_total` and let the porcelain render one marker. **Second, per-op failure never fails the batch** — `OpOutcome` is Result-shaped per index, mirroring `PartialSuccess`'s completed/failed/skipped (finding 21) while keeping positional indexing that `Vec<String>` loses. **Third, one `Provenance` for the batch**, which is only sound because of the snapshot; it also makes proposal 4's `ws.is_current()` a single call per briefing instead of N. **Fourth, `Detail` on the ops that support it**, so the budget can degrade before it drops (finding 2) — Monokl already has `symbols --lite`, so this is formalizing an existing capability, not new work.

Implementation note: `apply_budget` currently tokenizes every candidate block with tiktoken before deciding. Across a 10-op batch that is the dominant cost. Prefilter by `code.len()` bytes (already free) and only tokenize candidates that survive the byte filter — the existing loop already tracks both, so this is a reordering, not a redesign.

**Proposal 6 — split raw-analysis API from agent-facing API: confirm, and go further than proposed.**

rust-analyzer and git both draw this line, and rust-analyzer draws it harder than proposal 6 does: not two method families on one type, but **two crates**, with the presentation types *not shared* (finding 8). Monokl violates this today — `types.rs` derives `Serialize` on the core result types, and `output.rs` puts `serde_json` and `println!` in the library (finding 10).

Answer to question **(d)**:

- **`monokl-core` (plumbing).** `Workspace`, `Analysis` snapshots, `Arc<FileAnalysis>`, the import graph and symbol index, `LanguageAnalyzer`, and *fully ranked, deduped, uncapped* results. No `tiktoken`, no serde derives on result types, no caps, no rendered strings, no `println!`. Stable interface, because Wisp is a scripted consumer (finding 9). This is where `ws.analysis(path) -> Arc<FileAnalysis>` lives.
- **`monokl-agent` (porcelain).** `Budget`, `BudgetPolicy`, `apply_budget`, tiktoken, the `Detail` degrade path, truncation marker rendering, Michi integration, the CLI, and the MCP server if there is one. Owns the wire types and converts by hand from `monokl-core`'s POD types. Free to churn.

**Do Monokl's 50/500 symbol caps belong in the library? No — but the *ranking* does.** The distinction matters and the proposal blurs it. `pipeline::symbols`'s `per_file_cap = 50` / `total_cap = 500` are pure policy on an unordered set: nothing distinguishes the 50 symbols kept from the ones dropped, so the cap destroys information for no analytical reason. Delete them from the library outright. `budget::apply_budget`'s `max_results = 50` is different — it truncates a **BM25-ranked** list, so "the first 50" is a meaningful answer. Keep the ranking in `monokl-core` (`search()` returns the full ranked `Vec<RankedBlock>`); move the cutting to `monokl-agent`, with no defaults baked into the function. `Budget::agent_default()` in the porcelain crate can hold today's 50 / 20,000 / 2 MiB. Per Anthropic's guidance the cap should be a parameter with a sensible default, and `response_format: concise | detailed` should be the agent-facing knob over it (finding 12).

Same treatment for `dependents`'s `Cap = 200`: `monokl-core` returns all dependents; `monokl-agent` cuts and reports.

**Proposal 9 — shared `orin-contracts` crate: refine.**

The permissive-license motive is sound and independent — Michi is AGPL, Monokl is AGPL, and a shared vocabulary crate that Wisp and third-party harness plugins can depend on needs to be permissive. But finding 8 cuts against putting *result types* in it: rust-analyzer's invariant is explicitly *"don't make it serializable. Instead, create a serializable counterpart in [the presentation crate] and manually convert between the two."* A shared serde-derived contracts crate pulls wire concerns back into the analysis layer, which is the thing the split exists to prevent.

Refinement: `orin-contracts` holds **vocabulary only** — `CapabilityPrecision`, `ContentHash`, `Diagnostic`/`DiagnosticKind`, `Provenance`, the `Truncation`/`BudgetReport` shape, and the pinned artifact JSON schemas. Value types, no behavior, serde-derived because they *are* the wire format. Monokl's rich result types (`SymbolsResult`, `RankedBlock`, `FileAnalysis`) stay in `monokl-core`, unshared and *not* `Serialize`; their wire counterparts are built in `monokl-agent`. The test: if a type is something Wisp and Monokl must *agree on the meaning of*, it goes in contracts; if it is something Monokl *computes*, it does not.

## Answers to the direct questions

**(b) One `wisp_brief` MCP tool, or several? — Three, not one, and not eight.**

The evidence is real but narrower than it looks. Findings 11–12 establish that *large catalogs* hurt (13.62% at full catalog vs 43.13% with retrieval; degradation past ~30 tools; ~9.5% average MCP degradation) and that consolidation is the right instinct. **No study ablates 1 vs 3.** So the literature rules out eight-plus and says nothing about the difference between one and three; that call is judgment, made on three concrete grounds:

1. **Sourcegraph, the closest analogue with real usage data, chose curation over collapse** (finding 14): eight tools on the default endpoint, thirteen behind `/.api/mcp/all`. They demoted `go_to_definition` and `find_references` — the exact operations Wisp would fold into a briefing — but kept them reachable.
2. **A single tool with a `mode` enum re-creates the tool-selection problem inside the input schema**, where it is worse: the agent still chooses, but from an under-described enum variant instead of a tool with its own description, `outputSchema`, and annotations.
3. **The three surfaces have genuinely different cost and cardinality.** A briefing is expensive and called once per stage; a freshness check is nearly free and called repeatedly; artifact read/write is a different trust class (canonical, mutating).

Recommended surface:

- **`wisp_brief`** — the composite. Takes a stage and an artifact reference, internally issues one Monokl `query(&[Op])` batch, and returns the cited briefing. Per finding 17 this is the "everything about X" call **nobody ships**, and per finding 13 its value is that the ten intermediate results never enter the model's context. Give it `response_format: concise | detailed` (finding 12) and `detail: lite | full` mapping onto `Op::Detail`.
- **`wisp_artifacts`** — list, read, validate, and write `spec@1`/`plan@1`/etc. Separate because it mutates and because it is the canonical-provenance surface.
- **`wisp_check`** — freshness/provenance verification against a `Provenance` the agent already holds. Cheap, high-frequency, and separating it means an agent can re-verify without re-paying for a briefing.

Namespace them all `wisp_*` per finding 12. And **Monokl should not ship a six-tool MCP server mirroring its six subcommands** — that is the Serena failure mode (finding 15). If Monokl exposes MCP at all, it should be one or two tools over the batch API.

**(c) What Michi needs to be the envelope for both Monokl batch results and Wisp briefings.**

Five additions. Michi's MCP serialization is already correct (finding 22); the gap is entirely in what `AgentResponse` can hold.

1. **Multi-section support — the blocking gap** (finding 19). Today `RenderTarget` is `Unset | Toon | Kv` and `render()` dispatches on whichever of `items()`/`kv_items()` ran last, so a 10-section response silently loses nine. Add a repeatable `section()`:

   ```rust
   pub struct Section {
       pub name: String,
       pub body: SectionBody,          // Toon { fields, rows } | Kv(Vec<KvItem>) | Text(String)
       pub returned_count: usize,
       pub total_count: Option<usize>, // Some(n) with n > returned_count ⇒ "there is more"
       pub truncated: bool,
   }
   impl AgentResponse { pub fn section(self, s: Section) -> Self; }
   ```

   Keep `items()`/`kv_items()` as the one-section sugar so nothing breaks — they become `section(Section::toon(...))` with the existing `type_name`.

2. **A response-level `BudgetReport` slot** (finding 20). Today the only envelope-level "there is more" signal is a bare `total_count: Option<usize>`, and Monokl's truncation information can only reach the agent as free-text `hint()`. Add `pub fn budget(self, b: BudgetReport) -> Self`, rendered once as a `budget:` KV block plus per-section `returned/total`. This is the **single top-level budget report across sections** that finding 18 shows nobody has — it is Michi's job precisely because Michi is the shared layer both Monokl and Wisp render through.

3. **A `Provenance` slot** — one per response, not one per row: fingerprint, precision, freshness class, version. Rendered as a KV block. Wisp's provenance-class rule and Monokl's `WorkspaceFingerprint` both land here, and per finding 7 a batch has exactly one because it has exactly one snapshot.

4. **Per-op outcome rendering, reusing `PartialSuccess`** (finding 21) rather than a new type — but widen `completed`/`skipped` from `Vec<String>` to something index-bearing so `results[i] ↔ ops[i]` survives into the rendered output.

5. **Populate `structuredContent` with the envelope, and ship an `outputSchema`** (finding 5). `to_call_tool_result()` already emits `structured_content` from `render(OutputFormat::Json)`; extend that JSON to carry `sections[]`, `budget`, and `provenance`, and use the existing `schemars` feature to publish the `outputSchema` so clients can validate — the spec makes conformance a MUST once a schema is declared.

**Explicit non-requirement:** do not add pagination cursors. MCP defines them only for list operations (finding 4), so a cursor on a `tools/call` result is a private convention the client will not honor. Truncation + counts + a refinement hint is the right signal, and it must never be Serena's "no content is returned" (finding 16).

## Recommendations not on the list

1. **Define the batch as executing against one immutable snapshot, and say so in the type.** `Workspace::query` should internally take an `Analysis`-style snapshot (rust-analyzer's `AnalysisHost`/`Analysis`, finding 8) so all N results are mutually consistent and share one `Provenance`. Without this, a 10-op batch on a long-lived daemon `Workspace` can straddle an edit and produce a self-contradictory briefing — a correctness bug that N separate calls at least make visible. This is a stronger argument for proposal 2 than the token budget, and it is not in the proposal.

2. **Dedupe identical ops within a batch.** DataLoader's per-request cache (finding 6) exists for exactly this. A briefing that asks for `Symbols{a.ts}` and later `Symbols{a.ts}` should compute once and return the same result at both indices. Cheap, and it preserves the index-parallel contract.

3. **Degrade detail before dropping results.** LSP 3.17's `workspaceSymbol/resolve` returns symbols without ranges and resolves lazily (finding 2). Monokl's existing `symbols --lite` is the same idea; promote it to a per-op `Detail` and let `apply_budget` step `Full → Lite` before it truncates. For a briefing, twenty lite symbols beat five full ones, and today's `apply_budget` has no such lever.

4. **Give `wisp_brief` a `response_format: concise | detailed` parameter.** Anthropic's guidance, with concise measured at roughly one-third the tokens (finding 12). Cheaper than guessing one budget for all callers.

5. **Add a deadline to `query()` and mark unfinished ops `Skipped { Deadline }`.** Batching introduces head-of-line blocking that N separate calls do not have — one pathological op stalls the briefing. LSP's `$/cancelRequest` exists for this class of problem (finding 2), and Monokl needs the in-process equivalent. Without it the batch's failure mode is strictly worse than the status quo.

6. **Write down the "never fail-closed on overflow" rule as a project principle.** Serena returns nothing when `max_answer_chars` is exceeded (finding 16). Monokl already does better. Make it explicit so neither Wisp nor a future Monokl op regresses to it.

7. **Consider streaming for the daemon case.** LSP's `partialResultToken` appends items via `$/progress` notifications (finding 2). Not needed for v1 CLI briefings, but if the daemon (proposal 1) ever serves an interactive client, the batch response is a large one-shot payload and this is the established alternative.

## Contradictions and open questions

- **The tool-count evidence does not reach the question actually being asked.** RAG-MCP, the chance-corrected paper, and MCPGAUGE all operate at 30–3,251 tools. Recommendation (b) — three tools rather than one — rests on Sourcegraph's product decision and on schema-design reasoning, not on measured ablation. If Wisp's Prism paired-evaluation harness (proposal 16) can afford it, a 1-vs-3 tool arm is a cheap and genuinely novel experiment.
- **Sourcegraph's behavior cuts both ways.** They pruned the default set (supports consolidation) *and* kept the full granular surface at a second endpoint (cuts against collapsing). The honest reading is "curate the default, keep the primitives reachable" — which for Wisp might mean `wisp_brief` by default with Monokl's finer ops reachable through a second endpoint or a `detail` escape hatch, not that the finer ops should not exist.
- **No prior art exists for allocating one token budget across N heterogeneous result sections** (finding 18). DataLoader batches without rationing; MCP and LSP have no cross-call budget; Sourcegraph and Serena are strictly per-tool. `BudgetPolicy` is therefore a guess. Ship `Proportional` as the default, make the policy a parameter, and measure on the proposal-10 benchmark rather than reasoning about it further.
- **Snapshot cost is unmeasured.** Recommendation 1 assumes a cheap immutable snapshot. rust-analyzer gets this from salsa; Monokl refolds a `WorkspaceIndex` in memory per invocation and shares `Arc<FileAnalysis>` from a DashMap. Whether "snapshot" means an `Arc` clone of the index (cheap) or a rebuild (not cheap) depends on details of `WorkspaceIndex::build` I did not read. Worth confirming before the contract commits to it.
- **The exact MCPGAUGE degradation figure (~9.5%) was read from a search summary, not the paper.** Directionally corroborated by RAG-MCP's 13.62%-at-full-catalog, but do not quote the number without checking arXiv 2508.12566 directly.
- **Serena's `max_answer_chars` semantics come from a third-party schema mirror (glama.ai), not Serena's own docs.** The official tools page did not state overflow behavior. The quoted text reads like generated tool documentation and is probably accurate, but finding 16 is one confirmation short.
- **Whether `Op` should be an enum at all.** An enum forces every op into one dispatch and makes `OpResult` a parallel enum the caller must match twice. A trait-object or typed-builder alternative (each op knows its own result type) would be more Rust-idiomatic but breaks the homogeneous `&[Op]` slice and the index-parallel `Vec<OpOutcome>` that finding 6 argues for. I recommend the enum — the ordering contract is worth more than the type-level precision — but this is a real trade-off, not a settled one.

34	## Findings
35	
36	1. **PROJECTMEM's staleness rule is commit-distance over a decision's cited file, and it is advisory-with-human-adjudication, not blocking.** README: "Every decision that cites a file is cross-checked against that file's git history — when the file has moved on, the memory is *flagged* ("predates 7 commits to auth.py — confirm or supersede") and a human decides." The rendered precheck output shows the payload shape Wisp needs: subject path, a count, and the citing artifact's id — `decision [evt_9db5a3f8…] "auth uses session cookies, 30min timeout" — predates 7 commits`. There is no threshold constant in the README or paper; any N ≥ 1 flags. Source: README lines 296, 711-720.
37	
38	2. **The paper and the README disagree about what the mechanism is, and the README is the authoritative one for the staleness feature.** The paper's related-work section distinguishes PROJECTMEM from "Codified Context", whose "drift detector fires at *session start* from git-commit divergence, not from the project's logged failures and not *per action*", and describes PROJECTMEM's own gate as `precheck_file(path)` consulting the event log for failed attempts, open issues, and high churn — a path lookup, not a distance computation. The README documents both: `precheck` (event-log lookup) *and* stale-memory detection (commit distance, new in 0.1.4) as separate features surfaced in the same warning block. Treat them as two mechanisms, not one. **Consequence for Wisp: commit distance answers "is this evidence still trustworthy", and it is a different question from "has this artifact's own bytes changed".** Conflating them is the main modelling hazard here.
39	
40	3. **PROJECTMEM never deletes and never mutates: staleness is a flag, retirement is `--supersedes`, and the superseded event stays in the append-only log tagged forever.** `pjm decision "new way" --supersedes <id>`; MCP tool `add_decision(summary, supersedes?)`. Comparison table rows: "Stale memory: **flag, never delete**" and "Supersede without losing history", both marked unique versus 12 contemporary systems, which "silently decay or delete", "down-rank and prune via decay", "rewrite facts on update", or "self-edit in place".
41	
42	4. **PROJECTMEM's commit/gitignore split is: distilled outputs committed, raw log and runtime state gitignored.** Committed: `summary.md`, `PROJECT_MAP.md`, `AI_INSTRUCTIONS.md`, `issues/`, and `plan` ("It's committed (not gitignored) so intent is shared with your team"). Gitignored: `events.jsonl`, `watch.pid`, `watch.log`, and `structure.json` — the last described as "derived from code, gitignored, and never committed — code is only ever *read*." This is exactly Wisp's D-001/D-007 split (canonical artifacts committed, `.wisp/` derived cache gitignored) arrived at independently.
43	
44	5. **Silence is audited.** `pjm precheck --snooze 2h` "silences it politely — the snooze is itself logged, so even the silence is audited", and "every commit shows one dim line so silence is never mistaken for a clean check." This is the governing principle for Q-002's degradation path: a declined commit must be a recorded state, not an absent one.
45	
46	6. **No spec-driven tool in the survey detects staleness between its own artifacts by hash or link.** Spec Kit: `/speckit.plan` reads the spec, `/speckit.tasks` reads `plan.md` — no hash, no freshness marker, no version tracking; the doc's "Living Documentation" claim is a conceptual goal, not an implemented safeguard. Kiro: tasks carry requirement numbers (`1.1, 1.2, 1.3`), and re-sync is an explicit user action ("Sync Files", "Refine") — the tool does not notice on its own that `requirements.md` moved ahead of `tasks.md`. Martin Fowler's three-tool comparison contains no mention of hash-based versioning or drift detection for any of the three. **Wisp's `plan@1.spec_hash` mechanism is ahead of all three.**
47	
48	7. **Tessl's spec-as-source is the only one enforcing spec↔code linkage mechanically, and it does so by link integrity and ownership, not hashing.** Frontmatter `targets` declares the files a capability spec owns; requirements carry `**Verified by**: [@test] tests/path/test_file.py`. Three scripts enforce it: `check-spec-links.sh` (every `[@test]` resolves to an existing file), `check-target-ownership.sh` (a target file cannot change without its spec changing), `build-spec-manifest.py` (spec → requirements → targets → tests map). Semantic drift — "code does something the spec doesn't describe (or vice versa), despite links and tests being formally in place" — is explicitly left to an agent review, not automated. Two lessons: the manifest is built, not hardcoded; and the ownership check is *exactly* commit-distance over declared paths, which is Wisp proposal 13.
49	
50	8. **ADR tooling has a status lifecycle and a supersession pointer, but no code linkage and no drift detection at all.** MADR frontmatter: `status` ("proposed", "rejected", "accepted", "deprecated", or "superseded by ADR-0123"), `date` ("when the decision was last updated"), plus `decision-makers`/`consulted`/`informed`. Supersession is encoded *inside the status string*, not as a separate typed field — log4brains inherits this and requires the link text to be the target ADR's slug exactly, which its own maintainers call "too restrictive". "An ADR is immutable — only its status can change." **Do not copy the status-string encoding**; Wisp should carry `superseded_by` as its own typed field. PROJECTMEM's `--supersedes` (finding 3) is the better model because it is a first-class argument.
51	
52	9. **Backstage derives relations from typed schema fields rather than declaring edges in code — direct precedent for proposal 17.** "Entity descriptor YAML files are not supposed to contain this field. Instead, catalog processors analyze the entity descriptor data and its surroundings, and deduce relations." `spec.owner` → `ownedBy`, `spec.dependsOn` → `dependsOn`, `spec.providesApis` → `providesApi`, `spec.system` → `partOf`, each auto-reversed (`dependencyOf`). These are schema properties, not annotations, and the processor is generic. Backstage exposes `metadata.etag` for change detection but has no last-updated staleness banner or CI freshness check for entities or TechDocs.
53	
54	10. **Callisto already implements the exact git primitive Wisp needs, and its git crate is permissively licensed.** `callisto-vcs` and `callisto-model` are `MIT OR Apache-2.0`; only `callisto-graph` and the repo root LICENSE are AGPL-3.0-only. So `GitDataSource::commits_since(&self, since_ref: Option<&str>, pathspecs: &[PathBuf]) -> Result<Vec<GitCommit>, VcsError>` and its gix implementation `commits_since_with_pathspec(since: Option<&CommitSha>, pathspecs: &[PathBuf])` are reusable as code, not merely as a design pattern. **This materially narrows Q-003.**
55	
56	11. **The bounded-walk technique in that implementation is the reason it is cheap enough to run per artifact-link.** It uses `repo.rev_walk(vec![head.id]).with_hidden(Some(since_oid))` — gix's hidden-tip frontier algorithm, "exactly the same 'boundary commit' algorithm `git rev-list branch ^tag` itself uses" — instead of a second unbounded walk collected into an exclusion set, so "the walk stops once every in-flight branch has been resolved instead of continuing to the repository's first commit." Pathspecs "match as directory/path prefixes against a commit's tree diff vs. its first parent — mirrors `git log -- <pathspecs>`'s scoping, not full git pathspec magic"; merges are skipped. The crate instruments `REVWALK_VISIT_COUNT`, i.e. the authors treat walk cost as a measured budget.
57	
58	12. **gix exposes everything the freshness enum needs, at workspace granularity.** `Repository::rev_walk(spec) -> Result<RevWalk<'static>, Error>`, `status(options) -> Result<Status, Error>`, `index_worktree_status`, `tree_index_status`, `is_dirty() -> Result<bool, Error>`, `head_commit`, `head_tree_id`, `diff_tree_to_tree(old, new, options) -> Result<Vec<ChangeDetached>, Error>`. Note `is_dirty()` returns only a bool — the *set* of dirty paths, which `Freshness::DirtyAffected` requires, needs `status`/`index_worktree_status`.
59	
60	13. **OCI's digest grammar registers both SHA-256 and BLAKE3 under one prefixed format, and mandates SHA-256.** Grammar: `digest ::= algorithm ":" encoded`, `algorithm-component ::= [a-z0-9]+`, `encoded ::= [a-zA-Z0-9=_-]+`. Registered algorithm IDs: `sha256`, `sha512`, `blake3`. "Compliant implementations SHOULD use SHA-256" and "Implementations MUST implement SHA-256 digest verification for use in descriptors"; sha256 encoding is `/[a-f0-9]{64}/`. Implementations "SHOULD allow digests with unrecognized algorithms to pass validation if they comply with the above grammar." **This settles proposal 14: the prefix is not decoration, it is what lets one field carry both algorithms.**
61	
62	14. **Wisp's own docs currently contradict themselves on the hash algorithm.** `docs/02-architecture-and-contracts.md:58` says `blake3` with the rule "Hash raw persisted bytes when a contract requires a content hash", but the receipt example at line 163 is `"content_hash": "sha256:..."`, and `plan@1.spec_hash` in the shared schema specifies "Content hash (e.g. `sha256:<hex>`) of the spec@1 file". The schema is already shipped and consumed by `smith:recon`, so sha256 is the de-facto interchange hash and line 58 is the outlier.
63	
64	15. **The constitution already answers Q-002's core rule, twice, and Wisp's own doc already lists the four receipt states.** Constitution: "IF the spec is written to disk but not committed to version control, it SHALL be treated as not yet persisted — an uncommitted file is invisible to a fresh checkout, a future session, and drift-checker", and the same for plans. `docs/02-architecture-and-contracts.md:169-170`: "The operation must distinguish `validated`, `written_uncommitted`, `persisted`, and `commit_failed`. It cannot claim `persisted` when Git commit failed." Q-002's remaining live questions are therefore only: policy-file enforcement, and the no-Git-approval degradation path.
65	
66	16. **Idempotent-write tooling universally distinguishes no-op from applied, and Wisp's Milestone 1 gate implicitly requires the same.** kubectl reports `unchanged` when "the maintained configuration has not changed" versus `configured` when "kubectl submitted an update"; Ansible reports `ok` ("the desired state was already present or no change was needed") versus `changed`. Milestone 1's gate says "Re-running the same persistence request is idempotent **or** reports an exact, typed conflict" — with only the four states above, the idempotent branch is indistinguishable from a fresh write.
67	
68	17. **Tools that write files without committing treat that as a first-class mode, and at least one does it badly enough to be a cautionary tale.** cargo-release's dry-run "actually still makes changes to your working directory" — files modified, no commit, no tag — reported as issue #872 precisely because it "does a local commit with no feedback even in dry-run mode". Changesets makes committing opt-in config: "If you set the commit option in the config, the command will add the updated changeset files and then commit them" — i.e. write-only is the default and commit is the explicit escalation.
69	
70	18. **Callisto encodes the write/no-write boundary in the type system rather than a boolean, via a zero-sized capability token.** `pub struct ApplyPermit { _private: () }` with "the one sanctioned construction path: mints a permit unless a dry run was requested. `dry_run` should come straight from the parsed CLI flag, read exactly once near the top of a command handler. Recomputing or re-deriving it deeper in a call stack reintroduces the divergence this type exists to eliminate." Every ref-writing method takes `permit: &ApplyPermit`, so "a dry run has none to give and therefore cannot call this at all."
71	
72	19. **Identity-to-path has two opposed conventions in the field, and OpenSpec demonstrates the failure mode of the one Wisp did not pick.** OpenSpec derives identity from path — the hierarchical-structure proposal changes "the capability identifier from directory name to full relative path from `specs/`" — and its `openspec archive <change-id>` moves a change folder into `changes/archive/`, i.e. a routine lifecycle operation relocates the artifact and thereby changes its identity. Wisp's constitution takes the opposite convention: `<workspace_root>/docs/specs/<id>.json` and `docs/projects/<linked_spec>.json`, path derived from ID. Note that `plan@1`'s path is keyed by *another artifact's* id, so two plans for one spec collide by construction.
73	
74	20. **`x-` prefixed keywords are the forward-compatible way to declare links in a JSON Schema today.** They "are compatible with all versions of JSON Schema that are currently published; they'll still just be collected as annotations", so a validator that does not know them ignores them rather than failing. The formal route is a custom vocabulary declared in a dialect metaschema ("a database schema dialect might add keywords like `indexed` or `foreignKey`"), which buys enforcement but costs a metaschema and a custom validator. JSON Hyper-Schema's `links`/`rel`/`targetSchema` was the standardized answer but the 2020-12 hypermedia document 404s on json-schema.org and the vocabulary is effectively dormant — do not build on it.
75	
76	## Answers to the four questions asked
77	
78	### (a) Typed `Freshness` for Q-010
79	
80	The evidence says model this **per link, not per artifact** (finding 7: Tessl's ownership check is a spec→targets relation; finding 1: PROJECTMEM's rule is a decision→cited-file relation), and keep **two axes separate** (finding 2).
81	
82	```rust
83	/// Did the artifact's own bytes change since a consumer recorded them?
84	/// Answerable with no Git at all — this is `plan@1.spec_hash` generalized.
85	pub enum ArtifactFreshness {
86	    Matches { hash: ContentHash },
87	    Diverged { recorded: ContentHash, current: ContentHash },
88	    Missing { expected_path: Utf8PathBuf },
89	}
90	
91	/// Has the code this artifact-link points at moved on since the artifact was committed?
92	pub enum EvidenceFreshness {
93	    /// Worktree clean, HEAD == the commit that introduced the artifact.
94	    CleanAtCommit { commit: CommitSha },
95	    /// Worktree clean, HEAD has advanced but no commit touched the declared paths.
96	    CleanUnaffected { artifact_commit: CommitSha, head: CommitSha, commits_ahead: u32 },
97	    /// Worktree clean, N commits since the artifact touched declared paths.
98	    CleanBehind { artifact_commit: CommitSha, head: CommitSha, commits_touching: u32, touched_paths: Vec<Utf8PathBuf> },
99	    /// Worktree dirty, but no dirty path intersects the declared paths.
100	    DirtyUnaffected { head: CommitSha, dirty_path_count: usize },
101	    /// Worktree dirty and dirty paths intersect the declared paths.
102	    DirtyAffected { head: CommitSha, dirty_paths: Vec<Utf8PathBuf>, commits_touching: u32 },
103	    /// The artifact exists on disk but is not in any commit — commit distance is undefined.
104	    Uncommitted { path: Utf8PathBuf },
105	    /// No repository, shallow clone, or unresolvable artifact commit.
106	    Indeterminate { reason: FreshnessGap },
107	}
108	```
109	
110	Four refinements over the brief's four-state list, each earned by a source:
111	
112	- **`CleanBehind` carries `commits_touching`, not `commits_ahead`.** PROJECTMEM's message is "predates 7 commits **to auth.py**" — the count is filtered by path, which is what makes it actionable. An unfiltered distance-from-HEAD is noise in an active repo. Callisto's `commits_since_with_pathspec` computes exactly the filtered count (findings 1, 11).
113	- **`CleanUnaffected` must exist separately from `CleanAtCommit`.** Milestone 2's gate — "Editing an unrelated file does not invalidate an unrelated briefing" — is only expressible if "HEAD moved but not under my paths" is its own state.
114	- **`Uncommitted` is required, and it is the join point with Q-002.** An artifact in the `written_uncommitted` receipt state has no commit to measure distance from, so every other variant is a type error for it. Without this variant the implementation will silently fall back to `CleanAtCommit` and report a never-committed spec as current — precisely the failure the constitution's "an uncommitted file is invisible to a fresh checkout" rule exists to prevent (finding 15).
115	- **`Indeterminate` is required** because gix `rev_walk` errors, shallow clones, and detached/unborn HEAD are all reachable, and Wisp's provenance discipline forbids reporting an unknown as `Clean`.
116	
117	Deliberately **not** in the enum: any `Stale` boolean or threshold constant. No source uses a threshold (finding 1: any N ≥ 1 flags), and the stale/fresh judgment is the briefing profile's policy over this data, not a property of the data. Keep the enum descriptive and let `brief` decide what warns.
118	
119	Cost, per finding 11-12: one `Repository::status()` per workspace for the dirty-path set, and **one** `rev_walk` per distinct `since` commit with the **union** of all links' pathspecs, bucketed per link afterwards — not one walk per link. That is the concrete refinement to proposal 15.
120	
121	### (b) Persist receipt states for Q-002
122	
123	Keep `validated` / `written_uncommitted` / `persisted` / `commit_failed`, and add:
124	
125	- **`already_current`** — candidate's canonical bytes equal the bytes already at the destination, and that file is committed. Directly demanded by Milestone 1's "idempotent or reports an exact, typed conflict" gate and by universal precedent (finding 16: kubectl `unchanged`, Ansible `ok`). **This forces a pipeline reordering**: `docs/02-architecture-and-contracts.md:142-153` computes the content hash *after* the atomic write, so by the time the hash exists the evidence of a no-op has been overwritten. Canonicalize and hash the candidate *before* the temp-write, compare against the destination, and short-circuit.
126	- **`commit_declined { reason }`** — distinct from `commit_failed`. Q-002 asks for "how a harness with no Git write approval performs graceful degradation"; a refused approval is not an error and must not be reported as one, but per finding 5 it must be recorded rather than omitted. Reasons: `NotRequested`, `ApprovalDenied`, `NotARepository`, `PolicyDisabled`.
127	- **`conflict { existing_id, existing_path }`** — the other half of the Milestone 1 gate, and the enforcement point for Q-006 (see (e) below).
128	
129	`superseded` is *not* a receipt state — it is a lifecycle status on the artifact (findings 3, 8). Do not fold the two.
130	
131	One structural recommendation from finding 18: gate the commit behind an `ApplyPermit`-style zero-sized token minted once from the CLI flag plus harness approval, rather than threading a `bool commit` parameter. It makes `persisted`-without-a-commit unrepresentable instead of merely tested for, which is what the invariant "a receipt must never call an uncommitted file durable cross-session persistence" actually asks for.
132	
133	### (c) Schema extension keyword for proposal 17
134	
135	Use `x-wisp-link` as an annotation keyword now (finding 20: `x-` values are collected as annotations by every published JSON Schema version, so external validators and the direct-artifact fallback in `docs/02:172-178` keep working untouched). Defer a formal vocabulary + dialect metaschema until there is a second consumer.
136	
137	```json
138	"linked_spec": {
139	  "type": "string",
140	  "description": "ID of the spec@1 this plan implements",
141	  "x-wisp-link": { "target_type": "spec@1", "by": "id", "cardinality": "one", "resolution": "required" }
142	},
143	"spec_file_path": {
144	  "type": "string",
145	  "x-wisp-link": { "target_type": "spec@1", "by": "path", "cardinality": "one", "resolution": "required", "same_target_as": "linked_spec" }
146	},
147	"spec_hash": {
148	  "type": "string",
149	  "x-wisp-hash-of": { "link": "linked_spec", "algorithms": ["sha256"] }
150	}
151	```
152	
153	Two things this buys that nobody proposed. First, `same_target_as` makes the `linked_spec`/`spec_file_path` pair checkable — today nothing verifies that the id and the path name the same spec. Second, `x-wisp-hash-of` turns the constitution's Spec Staleness Detection rule from a plan→spec special case into a generic one: any field declared as the hash of a link becomes an `ArtifactFreshness` check for free, so `arch-model@1` or a future `brief` artifact inherits drift detection without new Rust. Backstage is the precedent that a generic processor over typed schema fields is sufficient (finding 9).
154	
155	Also declare paths in the schema rather than in Rust, which is what Q-006 needs (see (e)):
156	
157	```json
158	"$id": "plan@1",
159	"x-wisp-artifact": { "id_field": "linked_spec", "path_template": "docs/projects/{linked_spec}.json" }
160	```
161	
162	### (d) Is `sha256:`-prefixed SHA-256 the right interchange hash?
163	
164	Yes, and finding 13 makes the case stronger than "portable": OCI's `algorithm ":" encoded` grammar registers `sha256`, `sha512`, **and `blake3`** as sibling algorithm IDs. So the prefix is not a label on a sha256 field — it is the mechanism that lets one `content_hash` field carry `blake3:…` for an internal cache key and `sha256:…` for an interchange value without a second field or a format break. Adopt the OCI grammar verbatim, require `sha256` for anything crossing a process boundary (`plan@1.spec_hash` already does, finding 14), and permit `blake3:` internally.
165	
166	Two consequences. **Fix `docs/02-architecture-and-contracts.md:58`** — it currently mandates blake3 for "raw persisted bytes when a contract requires a content hash", which contradicts both the receipt example six lines from the schema it implements and the already-shipped `plan@1.spec_hash` (finding 14). The rule should read: sha256 for canonical artifact hashes in receipts and artifact fields, blake3 for `.wisp/` cache keys. **And specify what is hashed**: the constitution already says "over the raw file bytes as read from disk — not a parsed or re-serialized form", so the receipt's `content_hash` must be raw destination bytes post-write, which is consistent with the pipeline at line 149 but must survive the `already_current` reordering in (b) — hash the canonical candidate bytes, and they are by construction the bytes that will be written.
167	
168	### (e) Q-006 identity and path mapping
169	
170	Keep ID as the authority with path derived (constitution's `docs/specs/<id>.json`), not OpenSpec's path-derived identity — finding 19 shows the latter breaks on the tool's own archive operation. Declare the mapping in schema (`x-wisp-artifact.path_template`, above) so there is literally one public path-resolution table and it is data.
171	
172	Enforce bijection at write time in `artifact persist`: before the temp-write, if the destination exists, parse it and compare its id field; a mismatch returns `conflict { existing_id, existing_path }` rather than overwriting. This is the write-time enforcement Q-006 asks for and no surveyed tool implements. Note the specific hazard finding 19 identifies: `plan@1`'s path is keyed by `linked_spec`, so two plans for one spec are a guaranteed collision, and the constitution's amendment rule ("SHALL overwrite the existing file at the same plan_file_path") makes that intentional — so for `plan@1` the conflict check must compare `linked_spec`, and an equal `linked_spec` is an amendment (allowed overwrite), not a conflict.
173	
174	## Verdict on proposed changes
175	
176	**13 — Freshness as a typed value on commit distance: confirm, with refinement.** The only two systems in the survey that mechanically check artifact-vs-code currency both do it this way (PROJECTMEM's "predates 7 commits to auth.py", Tessl's `check-target-ownership.sh`), and no spec-driven tool does better. Refinements: split into two axes (`ArtifactFreshness` bytes-changed vs `EvidenceFreshness` code-moved) because PROJECTMEM's own paper and README show these are separate mechanisms; make the count path-filtered, not distance-from-HEAD; add `CleanUnaffected`, `Uncommitted`, and `Indeterminate` to the brief's four states; carry no threshold constant.
177	
178	**14 — SHA-256 for canonical hashes, blake3 for cache keys: confirm, strengthened.** OCI registers both under one prefixed grammar and mandates sha256 for interchange, so the split is standard rather than a compromise. Concrete action beyond the proposal: `docs/02-architecture-and-contracts.md:58` currently says the opposite and must be corrected — it contradicts the receipt example at line 163 and the shipped `plan@1.spec_hash`.
179	
180	**17 — Link declarations in schema metadata, not hardcoded Rust: confirm.** Backstage derives all catalog relations from typed spec fields via a generic processor and explicitly forbids hand-declared edges; Tessl builds its spec→requirements→targets→tests manifest from frontmatter with a script. Refinement: use `x-wisp-link` annotations (works with every published JSON Schema draft, does not break the direct-artifact fallback) rather than a custom vocabulary or JSON Hyper-Schema, which is dormant. Extend the idea to `x-wisp-hash-of` and `x-wisp-artifact.path_template` so freshness checking and path resolution are also data.
181	
182	**Q-002 — commit policy: refine.** The core rule is already decided (constitution, twice) and the four states are already in Wisp's doc. What is missing: `already_current` (Milestone 1's idempotency gate cannot be met without it), `commit_declined` distinct from `commit_failed` (the no-approval degradation path Q-002 explicitly asks about), and `conflict`. Precedent for the write-without-commit default is Changesets (commit is opt-in config) and cargo-release (dry-run writes files) — and cargo-release's issue #872 is the warning that write-without-commit must be *reported*, not silent.
183	
184	**Q-006 — identity and path mapping: refine.** Keep ID→path (OpenSpec's inverse convention breaks under its own `archive` command). Move the table into schema metadata. Enforce at write time by parsing the existing destination's id and returning a typed `conflict`; special-case `plan@1` where equal `linked_spec` means amendment, not collision.
185	
186	**Q-010 — freshness semantics for dirty worktrees: refine.** Answer is the `EvidenceFreshness` enum in (a). The brief's four cases are right but incomplete; `Uncommitted` in particular is load-bearing because it is where Q-002 and Q-010 meet, and omitting it makes a never-committed artifact report as current.
187	
188	## Recommendations not on the list
189	
190	1. **Reuse `callisto-vcs` directly rather than reimplementing the walk.** It is `MIT OR Apache-2.0` (only `callisto-graph` and the root LICENSE are AGPL), so Q-003's licensing concern does not apply to the one crate Wisp actually wants. `commits_since_with_pathspec` already handles the branchy-history correctness case that a naive two-walk-and-exclude implementation gets wrong, and its doc comment explains why. This is a week of subtle work already done and tested.
191	
192	2. **Adopt the `ApplyPermit` pattern for the commit step.** Zero-sized token minted once from the flag, required by every mutating call. Q-002's minimum invariant ("a receipt must never call an uncommitted file durable cross-session persistence") is currently a test; this makes it a compile error.
193	
194	3. **Record declined commits and suppressed warnings, and surface them.** PROJECTMEM logs its own snooze and prints "one dim line so silence is never mistaken for a clean check." Wisp's briefing should carry the same: a `commit_declined` artifact and a suppressed freshness warning must both appear in the briefing's gap list, or the bounded-context guarantee (D-008) leaks.
195	
196	4. **Add `superseded_by` as a typed field on artifact schemas, not a status string.** MADR and log4brains both encode supersession inside the status string and log4brains' maintainers document the resulting brittleness. PROJECTMEM's `--supersedes <id>` argument is the better shape. Wisp has no supersession model at all today; the `spec_contradiction` → corrected-spec loop overwrites in place, which means the superseded version exists only in Git history and cannot be cited by a briefing.
197	
198	5. **Instrument the walk budget.** Callisto keeps a `REVWALK_VISIT_COUNT` atomic. Wisp's briefing compiler should carry commits-visited in its truncation/provenance record, so "freshness cost" is measurable before it becomes the reason a briefing is slow.
199	
200	6. **The `spec_hash` field generalizes to a `linked_hash` on every link.** Only `plan@1` carries a hash of its source today. Any artifact citing another by id should be able to pin the bytes it read, which is what makes finding 6's advantage over Spec Kit/Kiro durable rather than accidental.
201	
202	## Contradictions and open questions
203	
204	1. **PROJECTMEM's paper and README describe different mechanisms** (finding 2). The paper's text positions commit-divergence drift detection as a *competitor's* approach while the README ships it as a 0.1.4 feature. Most likely explanation: the paper describes the pre-action gate and the README describes gate + staleness as two features; the paper may predate 0.1.4. I could not resolve this from the sources — the paper HTML has no staleness-algorithm section at all. Neither source gives the actual implementation (no source file was read), so the exact definition of "commits to auth.py" — first-parent tree diff, rename-following, merge handling — is **unverified**. Callisto's implementation is the one whose semantics I can quote precisely.
205	
206	2. **No threshold constant found anywhere.** PROJECTMEM flags at any N ≥ 1 as far as the README shows, but neither source states this explicitly. If Wisp wants a warn-threshold, there is no precedent to copy and it should be config, not a constant.
207	
208	3. **Kiro's sync behavior is only lightly sourced.** `kiro.dev/docs/specs/concepts/` returned 404 and I relied on search snippets plus Martin Fowler's comparison. The claim "Kiro has no automatic staleness detection between requirements/design/tasks" is *likely*, not confirmed — though Fowler's article explicitly containing no mention of drift detection for any of the three tools is reasonable corroboration.
209	
210	4. **Tessl's `check-target-ownership.sh` mechanism is described but not read.** "Prevents target files from changing without spec updates" — whether that is a git-diff comparison in CI, a commit-distance check, or a mtime check is unstated in the fetched summary. If it matters, the tile repo (`github.com/tesslio/spec-driven-development-tile`) has the scripts.
211	
212	5. **Changesets' current commit semantics are unverified.** The page fetched is self-marked outdated and redirects to `changesets.dev/guide/cli`, which I did not fetch. The claim "commit is opt-in config" holds for the version documented there.
213	
214	6. **Whether `blake3` is worth keeping at all is open.** If `.wisp/` cache keys are the only blake3 consumer and briefings are dominated by git and Monokl cost, a single sha256 everywhere removes a dependency and a class of "which hash is this field" bugs. No evidence either way on whether Wisp's hashing volume justifies two algorithms — that is a measurement, not a literature question.
215
